sections.heading: 27. Summary
sections.text:
Reranking remains useful in modern agent systems because efficient first-stage retrieval and precise relevance judgment are different optimization problems.

The the platform position is not that every retrieval pipeline needs a reranker.

It is:

> Retrieve broadly enough to preserve useful evidence, then spend additional ranking compute only when doing so improves the information ultimately delivered to the agent.

The effectiveness of reranking should be judged by the complete system outcome: better evidence, smaller and cleaner context, greater task success, acceptable latency, and lower or justified total cost.

sections.heading: 1. Summary
sections.text:
Progressive disclosure is the practice of exposing only enough information for an agent to determine the next useful action, while keeping deeper instructions, references, tools, and supporting material discoverable on demand.

The objective is not to make context small for its own sake. The objective is to keep **active context relevant, authoritative, and economical** while preserving access to a much larger body of knowledge and capability.

the platform currently recommends progressive disclosure as the default design pattern for large reusable instruction sets, skills, repository guidance, tool catalogs, and organizational knowledge.

The default should be:

```text
small stable core
      ↓
capability metadata
      ↓
agent selects relevant capability
      ↓
load focused instructions
      ↓
retrieve supporting references as needed
      ↓
execute and verify
```

rather than:

```text
load every rule
load every skill
load every tool description
load every reference
load every repository convention
      ↓
ask the model to ignore what does not matter
```

sections.heading: 2. Why Progressive Disclosure Matters
3. Progressive Disclosure Is Not Lazy Loading Alone
sections.text:
Progressive disclosure is sometimes described as "lazy loading for prompts." That analogy is useful but incomplete.

The design has at least four responsibilities:

1. **Discovery** — the agent must know that useful information or capability exists.
2. **Selection** — the agent must determine when that capability is relevant.
3. **Expansion** — the system must load the appropriate detail when selected.
4. **Retention** — the system must decide what remains active after the information has served its purpose.

A system that defers loading but provides poor discovery metadata can fail because the agent never realizes the required knowledge exists.

A system that discovers correctly but never releases obsolete material can still accumulate context bloat.

Progressive disclosure is therefore a **context lifecycle pattern**, not merely a file-loading optimization.

sections.heading: 4. The the platform Disclosure Model
sections.text: the platform should distinguish at least four levels of disclosure.

sections.heading: Level 0 — Governing Context
Level 1 — Discovery Metadata
Level 2 — Operational Guidance
Level 3 — Supporting Evidence and Deep Reference
5. Disclosure as a Funnel
sections.text:
The model can be represented as:

```text
                    Governing context
                         small
                          │
                          ▼
                  discovery metadata
                          │
                  ┌───────┴───────┐
                  ▼               ▼
             capability A     capability B
                  │
                  ▼
             operational
              guidance
                  │
          ┌───────┴────────┐
          ▼                ▼
      reference       reference
         A1               A2
```

The number of available resources may be large while the active working set remains relatively small.

This is a key architectural property: **the total knowledge available to an agent need not equal the knowledge occupying its context window.**

sections.heading: 6. Repository Instructions
7. Skills
sections.text:
Skills are a natural progressive-disclosure boundary.

A skill should expose enough metadata for reliable selection without forcing its full contents into context.

Recommended structure:

```text
skills/
  postgres-migration/
    SKILL.md
    references/
      rollback.md
      zero-downtime.md
      prisma.md
    scripts/
      validate-migration.sh
    templates/
      migration-plan.md
    evals/
```

The root `SKILL.md` should usually remain a focused operational router.

It should explain:

- when to use the skill;
- when not to use it;
- required preconditions;
- high-level workflow;
- mandatory verification;
- relevant supporting files;
- approval boundaries.

Detailed reference information should live in supporting material that can be read selectively.

sections.heading: Anti-pattern: The Giant Skill
sections.text:
```text
SKILL.md
  8,000 lines
  every possible workflow
  every API reference
  every troubleshooting case
  every example
```

This undermines the purpose of skills by turning activation into a large context injection.

sections.heading: Preferred pattern
sections.text:
```text
SKILL.md
  concise workflow + routing

references/
  migration-design.md
  rollback.md
  prisma.md
  postgres-locking.md
```

The skill tells the agent **where to look**, not everything it could ever know.

sections.heading: 8. Tools and Progressive Disclosure
sections.text:
Tool availability also consumes context because agents need enough description to understand which tools exist and when to call them.

Large static tool catalogs can therefore become another form of context bloat.

Tool systems should support some combination of:

- compact tool descriptions;
- capability grouping;
- dynamic discovery;
- contextual tool registration;
- scoped MCP servers;
- cached capability catalogs;
- task-specific tool exposure.

The July 2026 MCP specification strengthens this architecture by making discovery optional and list responses cacheable. Clients can retrieve server capabilities when needed and cache tool/resource catalogs according to server-provided freshness hints.

This enables a useful pattern:

```text
agent knows:
  "repository tools are available"

        ↓
needs repository operation

        ↓
discover repository capabilities

        ↓
load relevant tool definitions

        ↓
call selected tool
```

However, discovery itself has cost. Systems should not rediscover stable capabilities repeatedly when safe caching or static registration is more efficient.

sections.heading: 9. Knowledge Bases and Handbook Retrieval
sections.text:
The the platform handbook should use the same pattern.

The future knowledge service should avoid returning complete chapters unless explicitly requested.

Instead:

```text
task
  ↓
resolve applicable knowledge domains
  ↓
return compact guidance summaries + provenance
  ↓
agent requests deeper guidance if needed
  ↓
retrieve specific sections / experiments / references
```

A future response might initially contain:

```yaml
applicable_guidance:
  - id: AEP-CTX-007
    title: Progressive Disclosure
    status: recommended
    summary: Load reusable guidance only when task relevance is established.

  - id: AEP-SEC-004
    title: Tool Authority Boundaries
    status: approved
    summary: Production write access requires explicit approval.
```

The agent can then request the complete section only when required.

This is preferable to injecting the entire handbook into every task.

sections.heading: 10. Discovery Metadata Is an Interface
sections.text:
Metadata quality becomes extremely important in progressive systems.

Poor description:

```yaml
name: database
description: Helps with databases.
```

Better description:

```yaml
name: postgres-migration
description: >-
  Create, modify, review, and validate PostgreSQL schema migrations.
  Use for migration files, rollout planning, rollback design, lock-risk
  analysis, and schema-change verification. Do not use for ordinary query
  optimization or application-level database access.
```

The second version improves both positive and negative routing.

Good discovery metadata should communicate:

- what capability exists;
- when it applies;
- when it does not apply;
- important boundaries;
- where deeper material lives.

Metadata should be treated as a **machine-facing API contract**, not merely documentation.

sections.heading: 11. Agent-Directed Exploration
sections.text:
Progressive disclosure does not require centralized retrieval for every decision.

Agents with filesystem, search, and shell capabilities can often discover context effectively through exploration.

For example:

```text
inspect repository root
      ↓
read package.json
      ↓
identify Nx workspace
      ↓
query Nx project graph
      ↓
inspect target project
      ↓
load framework-specific skill
      ↓
read only affected files
```

This can outperform prematurely retrieving large amounts of repository context.

However, exploration can also become inefficient.

Failure modes include:

- repeatedly inspecting the same locations;
- following irrelevant directory trees;
- reading excessively large files;
- missing important but non-obvious sources;
- using many tool calls where indexed retrieval would have been cheaper;
- failing to record discoveries for later steps.

Progressive disclosure therefore works best when agents have **good navigation affordances and stopping heuristics**.

sections.heading: 12. Push vs Pull Context
sections.text: Context can enter the agent through two broad mechanisms.

sections.heading: Push
Pull
13. Progressive Disclosure and Security
14. Context Retention After Disclosure
sections.text:
Loading information on demand solves only half the problem.

A long-running agent may eventually accumulate every disclosed item anyway.

The system therefore needs retention rules.

Possible approaches include:

- retain while the associated task phase is active;
- retain only a compact summary;
- move detailed material back to retrievable state;
- preserve a structured pointer rather than raw content;
- retain immutable decisions while dropping exploratory evidence;
- rely on prompt caching for stable prefixes where appropriate;
- compact completed subtask histories.

Example:

```text
Database migration skill loaded
        ↓
migration implemented + verified
        ↓
retain:
  - migration decision
  - verification result
  - relevant file paths

discard from active context:
  - full migration tutorial
  - unused examples
  - transient command output
```

This concept should be developed further in AEP-CTX-008 and AEP-CTX-009.

sections.heading: 15.1 Over-disclosure
15.2 Under-disclosure
15.3 Bad Discovery Metadata
sections.text: Capabilities exist but their descriptions are vague, overlapping, or misleading.

sections.heading: 15.4 Disclosure Cascades
sections.text:
Selecting one capability automatically loads many additional resources regardless of need.

Example:

```text
load AWS skill
   ↓
loads IAM + EKS + Lambda + SQS + RDS + Terraform + CloudWatch docs
```

This recreates static context bloat under a different name.

sections.heading: 15.5 Permanent Accumulation
sections.text: Resources are progressively loaded but never removed or compacted.

sections.heading: 15.6 Retrieval Without Authority Awareness
sections.text:
Relevant information is retrieved even though the current task or identity should not have access to it.

Authorization must occur before relevance ranking.

sections.heading: 15.7 Excessive Discovery Calls
sections.text: An agent repeatedly enumerates stable skills or tools instead of using cached capability information.

sections.heading: 15.8 Over-engineered Routing
sections.text: Complex classifiers and routing models are introduced for cases where a short list of clearly described capabilities would allow the primary agent to select reliably.

sections.heading: 16. When Eager Loading Is Better
17. A Practical Disclosure Budget
sections.text: the platform should eventually define workload-specific budgets, but a useful qualitative model is:

sections.heading: Always active
sections.text: Only material that is broadly applicable and high consequence.

sections.heading: Discoverable metadata
sections.text: Enough information to route confidently.

sections.heading: Active working set
sections.text: Material required for the current phase of work.

sections.heading: Externalized state
sections.text: Important information preserved outside active context.

sections.heading: Recoverable archive
sections.text:
Detailed history or references available if needed later.

Conceptually:

```text
                      total available knowledge
                               huge
                                │
                         recoverable archive
                                │
                         externalized state
                                │
                       active working context
                                │
                         governing context
                               small
```

sections.heading: 18. Recommended platform Pattern
sections.text:
For coding agents, the current recommended baseline is:

```text
1. Load governing policy and task objective.

2. Load compact repository guidance.

3. Expose capability metadata for available skills/tools.

4. Let the agent inspect the environment and identify task class.

5. Load only relevant skills.

6. Retrieve task-specific knowledge and repository context.

7. Execute using deterministic tools where possible.

8. Preserve decisions and verification state.

9. Compact or release detailed context after the corresponding phase.

10. Reload deeper references when later evidence requires them.
```

sections.heading: 19. Relationship to `AGENTS.md`
sections.text:
For the platform repositories, `AGENTS.md` should generally operate as a **bootstrap and routing layer**.

Recommended responsibilities:

```text
AGENTS.md
├── repository identity
├── permanent constraints
├── build/test/lint entry points
├── authority restrictions
├── project-discovery guidance
├── available skill locations
└── pointers to deeper standards
```

Avoid turning `AGENTS.md` into:

```text
the platform engineering handbook
+ React handbook
+ AWS handbook
+ security handbook
+ deployment handbook
+ project history
+ troubleshooting encyclopedia
```

This distinction is especially important because improvements in model capability can make old scaffolding unnecessary. OpenAI's September 2026 guidance explicitly recommends revisiting accumulated skill and `AGENTS.md` instructions rather than retaining complexity written to compensate for earlier model limitations.

sections.heading: 20. Relationship to MCP
sections.text:
A future the platform MCP knowledge service should support progressive disclosure natively.

Potential capability flow:

```text
server/discover
      ↓
knowledge domains
      ↓
resolve_guidance(task, scope)
      ↓
compact applicable guidance
      ↓
get_guidance(id, section?)
      ↓
get_reference(id)
```

This is preferable to a single tool such as:

```text
search_everything(query)
```

because the knowledge service should understand provenance, authority, scope, maturity, and applicability—not merely textual similarity.

sections.heading: 21. Evaluation
sections.text:
Progressive disclosure should be evaluated end-to-end rather than only by token count.

Relevant metrics include:

sections.heading: Quality
Efficiency
Behavioral quality

sections.heading: OpenAI — Agent Skills
sections.text:
Current OpenAI documentation describes skills as directories containing a `SKILL.md` manifest and supporting resources. In Agents API sessions, discovered skill names and descriptions are added to context; the model can then select a relevant skill and read its full instructions and supporting files.

Source: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-skills

sections.heading: OpenAI — Rethinking Skills and Prompts for GPT-6 Astra
sections.text:
OpenAI's September 11, 2026 guidance identifies progressive disclosure as a key property of useful skills and recommends making the root skill document a minimal router for larger workflows. It also recommends revisiting accumulated prompts and repository instructions as model capabilities improve.

Source: https://developers.openai.com/blog/rethinking-skills-and-prompts-for-gpt-6-astra

sections.heading: Anthropic — Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents
sections.text:
Anthropic describes progressive disclosure as allowing agents to incrementally discover relevant context through exploration while maintaining only necessary information in working memory. It also notes the tradeoff between runtime exploration and precomputed retrieval.

Source: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

sections.heading: Anthropic — Agent Skills
sections.text:
Anthropic's skill architecture uses metadata as a first disclosure layer, the main `SKILL.md` as a second layer, and supporting resources as additional layers that can be read only when necessary.

Source: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills

sections.heading: Model Context Protocol — 2026-07-28 Specification
sections.text:
The current MCP specification supports optional capability discovery and cacheable list/resource results, enabling clients to avoid repeatedly injecting or fetching complete capability catalogs while still discovering them when required.

Source: https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/

sections.heading: 26. Current Conclusion
sections.text:
Progressive disclosure should be considered a foundational the platform context-engineering pattern.

The central principle is:

> **Make important capabilities discoverable before making their full contents active.**

This allows the system's available knowledge and capability surface to grow significantly without requiring the active context window to grow at the same rate.

The remaining engineering challenge is not whether progressive disclosure is useful, but **where to place the disclosure boundaries, how to make discovery reliable, and when the additional retrieval overhead stops being worthwhile.**

sections.heading: 1. Summary
sections.text:
Long-running agents eventually accumulate more conversational history, tool output, reasoning residue, intermediate plans, failures, and stale details than should remain in active model context.

Context compression and compaction are therefore not merely token-saving techniques. They are mechanisms for **preserving continuity while reducing active-context load**.

the platform currently recommends that long-running agents separate three concerns:

1. **durable history** — recoverable source material and execution history;
2. **working state** — explicit structured state required to continue the task;
3. **active context** — the compact set of information supplied to the model for the current step.

The preferred architecture is therefore:

```text
raw history + artifacts + trace
            │
            ├───────────────┐
            │               │
            ▼               ▼
     structured state    retrievable history
            │               │
            └───────┬───────┘
                    ▼
              compaction
                    │
                    ▼
              active context
```

Compaction should reduce redundancy and stale detail without making important history unrecoverable.

sections.heading: 2. Current State of Practice
sections.text:
Modern agent platforms increasingly provide first-class compaction because long-running tasks can span multiple context windows.

OpenAI's current Responses API supports both automatic server-side compaction and an explicit standalone compaction endpoint. The resulting compacted context carries forward prior state in a smaller representation while allowing the application to continue a long-running workflow. OpenAI also recommends compaction after meaningful milestones so obsolete tool logs, retries, and abandoned branches do not crowd out the state needed for later work.

The OpenAI Agents API likewise automatically compacts earlier context as long-running sessions approach context limits.

Anthropic describes compaction as one of several context-management techniques for long-horizon work, alongside structured memory and sub-agent architectures. Anthropic's long-running-agent guidance also emphasizes that compaction by itself is insufficient: agents need external state, incremental work, tests, artifacts, and explicit progress tracking so they can recover across context resets.

These systems support a common conclusion:

> Long-running continuity should not depend on retaining an ever-growing transcript verbatim in active context.

sections.heading: 3. Compression, Summarization, and Compaction
sections.text: These terms overlap but should be distinguished.

sections.heading: Compression
Summarization
sections.text:
A lossy natural-language transformation intended to preserve the important meaning of a larger source.

Example:

```text
120 turns of debugging history
        ↓
"The failure was narrowed to stale IAM credentials. Attempts A and B failed;
refresh-on-connection is the remaining hypothesis."
```

Summaries are useful but can omit details, introduce interpretation, or erase uncertainty.

sections.heading: Compaction
sections.text:
A broader context-management operation that replaces or transforms accumulated active context into a smaller continuation state.

Compaction may use summarization internally, but it can also preserve structured state, selected verbatim items, opaque model-native state, artifact references, or other representations.

the platform should therefore avoid assuming that **compaction = one prose summary**.

sections.heading: 4. The Principal Risk: Silent Information Loss
5. the platform State Classification
sections.text: Before compacting context, agents should classify information by persistence needs.

sections.heading: A. Governing constraints
B. Decisions
C. Current working state
D. Evidence and observations
E. Ephemeral process history
6. Structured State Before Prose Summary
sections.text:
Where information has a stable schema, prefer structured state.

Instead of:

```text
We tried several things and eventually determined that the API implementation
works, but the integration test still fails because the fixture uses the old
schema, and we still need to update that plus rerun lint and typecheck.
```

prefer:

```yaml
phase: implementation
completed:
  - api implementation
remaining:
  - update integration fixture
  - run lint
  - run typecheck
known_failures:
  - test: customer-profile.integration
    cause: stale fixture schema
```

Structured state is easier to validate, diff, query, and selectively reload.

Narrative summaries remain useful for information that does not fit a rigid schema.

sections.heading: 7. Preserve Exact Information When Exactness Matters
8. Durable History and Recoverability
9. Checkpoint-Oriented Compaction
Reactive compaction
sections.text:
Triggered when the active context approaches a token threshold.

Advantages:

- easy to implement;
- protects against hard context exhaustion.

Limitations:

- compaction may occur at an awkward reasoning boundary;
- obsolete material may degrade performance long before the hard limit is reached.

sections.heading: Proactive compaction
11. Selective Retention
sections.text:
A compaction operation should conceptually decide among:

```text
retain verbatim
retain structurally
summarize
reference externally
discard from active context
```

This is more expressive than a binary keep/drop decision.

For example:

| Information | Preferred treatment |
|---|---|
| Task objective | retain verbatim/structured |
| Security boundary | retain verbatim/structured |
| Architecture decision | structured + brief rationale |
| Large log file | external reference |
| Exact current error | retain verbatim |
| Failed exploratory commands | usually discard |
| Old hypothesis | retain only if its rejection matters |
| Completed subtask details | summarize/reference |

sections.heading: 12. Context Rot
13. Tool Output Compression
sections.text:
Tool output is a major source of context growth.

Instead of returning a 20,000-line log directly to the model, deterministic code can often extract:

```yaml
exit_code: 1
failed_tests:
  - customer-profile.integration
first_relevant_error: "expected field 'status'"
artifact: artifacts/test-run-20260930.log
```

The full log remains available through the artifact reference.

This follows the broader principle:

> Move deterministic filtering and aggregation outside the model context whenever possible.

The model should receive enough information to reason, plus the ability to inspect the underlying source when necessary.

sections.heading: 14. Compaction and Retrieval
sections.text:
Compaction and retrieval are complementary.

Compaction determines what remains in the immediate continuation state.

Retrieval determines what older or external information should be restored when it becomes relevant again.

A mature long-running system therefore resembles:

```text
                     durable event/history store
                              │
                       retrieval/indexing
                              │
                              ▼
current task → structured state → active context
                     ▲              │
                     │              ▼
                     └──── compaction
```

This architecture reduces pressure on any single summary to preserve every potentially useful detail forever.

sections.heading: 15. Compaction and Memory
sections.text:
Compaction should not automatically promote temporary task information into long-term memory.

These are separate decisions.

Example:

```text
"Test X currently fails because fixture Y is outdated."
```

This may need to survive the next three context windows but should probably disappear once the task is completed.

By contrast:

```text
"This repository requires migrations to remain backward-compatible for one release."
```

may belong in durable repository guidance.

Compaction answers:

> What must survive this task's continuation?

Memory answers:

> What should remain available beyond this task?

sections.heading: 16. Compaction and Subagents
17. Compaction Quality Requirements
sections.text:
A compaction system should be evaluated for more than compression ratio.

Relevant metrics include:

sections.heading: State preservation
Downstream task success
sections.text: Does the agent still complete the task correctly after one or more compactions?

sections.heading: Recovery accuracy
sections.text: When an omitted detail becomes relevant later, can the agent retrieve the original information?

sections.heading: Token reduction
sections.text: How much active context is eliminated?

sections.heading: Latency
sections.text: What does compaction itself cost?

sections.heading: Monetary cost
sections.text: What model/tool cost is introduced?

sections.heading: Drift
sections.text: Does repeated compaction alter facts or progressively distort state?

sections.heading: 18. Repeated-Compaction Drift
sections.text:
Repeatedly summarizing summaries is especially risky.

Consider:

```text
raw history
   ↓
summary A
   ↓
summary B
   ↓
summary C
```

Each generation creates another opportunity for omission and reinterpretation.

Where possible, later compaction should have access to durable primary state rather than only the previous prose summary.

Prefer:

```text
raw durable state ──────┐
structured state ───────┼→ next compaction
latest working context ─┘
```

rather than indefinitely compressing already-compressed narrative.

sections.heading: 19. User and Human Visibility
sections.text:
Model-native compaction may be opaque, as in systems that carry internal compressed state not intended for human inspection.

For enterprise and enterprise engineering workflows, the platform should still maintain human-readable task state where auditing, handoff, approval, or debugging requires it.

A useful architecture can therefore maintain both:

```text
model-native continuation state
+
human-readable checkpoint state
+
durable trace/history
```

These solve different problems.

sections.heading: Summary becomes policy
sections.text:
A generated summary accidentally changes a tentative decision into a requirement.

**Mitigation:** preserve provenance and classification.

sections.heading: Constraint loss
sections.text:
A user or repository requirement disappears during compaction.

**Mitigation:** store governing constraints separately from general narrative.

sections.heading: Failure amnesia
sections.text:
The agent retries an already-rejected approach because the reason for rejection was lost.

**Mitigation:** preserve rejected approaches when they materially affect future choices.

sections.heading: Evidence laundering
sections.text:
A summary records a conclusion but loses the evidence/source that supported it.

**Mitigation:** retain evidence references.

sections.heading: Repeated-summary drift
sections.text:
Multiple generations progressively distort history.

**Mitigation:** re-ground compaction from durable state when possible.

sections.heading: Over-retention
sections.text:
The system technically compacts but keeps most stale information anyway.

**Mitigation:** measure active-context composition and token reduction.

sections.heading: Over-compression
sections.text:
Token savings are maximized at the expense of task continuity.

**Mitigation:** optimize downstream success, not compression ratio alone.

sections.heading: 21. Recommended platform Pattern
sections.text:
For long-running software-development agents, the initial recommended pattern is:

```text
1. Persist artifacts and execution history outside active context.

2. Maintain explicit structured task state:
   objective
   constraints
   decisions
   completed work
   remaining work
   known failures
   approvals
   artifact/evidence references

3. Keep recent, highly relevant interaction context verbatim.

4. Compact older process history at semantic checkpoints and token thresholds.

5. Preserve exact values that matter operationally.

6. Make compacted-away history retrievable where practical.

7. Rehydrate specific historical details only when needed.

8. Evaluate compaction using downstream task success and state-recall tests.
```

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-008-G1 — Treat compaction as state management, not text shortening
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Optimize for continued task correctness rather than maximum token reduction.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-008-G2 — Separate durable history from active context
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Do not require every potentially useful historical detail to remain in the model window.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-008-G3 — Preserve governing constraints explicitly
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Critical constraints and authority boundaries should not depend solely on lossy narrative summaries.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-008-G4 — Prefer structured state for structured facts
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Use schemas for decisions, tasks, failures, approvals, and artifact references where appropriate.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-008-G5 — Preserve exact values when paraphrase can alter meaning
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Identifiers, paths, errors, commands, hashes, and critical configuration should remain exact or externally referenced.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-008-G6 — Compact around meaningful milestones
sections.text:
**Status:** Provisional

Semantic checkpoints should complement hard token thresholds.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-008-G7 — Avoid repeated lossy summarization without re-grounding
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Repeated summary-of-summary compression should not become the sole source of truth.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-008-G8 — Keep discarded information recoverable when feasible
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Compaction should reduce active context without needlessly destroying historical evidence.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-008-G9 — Measure downstream success, not only compression ratio
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

A smaller context that causes more mistakes is not an improvement.

sections.heading: EXP-CTX-007 — Compaction Strategies
EXP-CTX-008 — Durable History With Selective Recall
sections.text:
Compare irreversible compacted history against an architecture retaining raw durable history plus selective retrieval.

Measure recovery from late-emerging dependencies and previously discarded details.

sections.heading: EXP-CTX-022 — Semantic Checkpoint vs Threshold-Only Compaction
sections.text:
Compare compaction triggered only by context thresholds with compaction performed at meaningful task milestones plus threshold fallback.

Hypothesis:

> Semantic checkpoint compaction reduces stale-context interference and preserves clearer task state without reducing correctness.

sections.heading: EXP-CTX-023 — Structured State vs Narrative Summary
24. Open Questions
sections.text:
1. Which information classes should always survive compaction verbatim?
2. How often should checkpoint state be regenerated?
3. What schema provides enough structure without becoming burdensome?
4. How should contradictions between durable history and compacted state be resolved?
5. When should the model itself decide that compaction is useful?
6. How much recent verbatim history should accompany compacted state?
7. How do provider-native compaction mechanisms compare with application-managed structured state?
8. How should compaction behave across multiple agents with separate context windows?
9. What metrics best detect semantic drift after repeated compactions?
10. When should compacted task state be promoted into durable organizational memory?

sections.heading: 26. Conclusion
sections.text:
Compaction is necessary because long-running agent work produces more history than should remain active at once.

But the goal is not simply to make history smaller.

The goal is to preserve **continuity, constraints, decisions, recoverability, and evidence** while removing stale process noise from active attention.

the platform should therefore treat context compaction as part of a broader state architecture:

> **durable history + structured working state + selective retrieval + compact active context**

That architecture gives agents room to work for long periods without requiring each new context window to forget how it got there.

sections.heading: 1. Summary
2. Memory Is Not the Context Window
sections.text:
A long-running agent session can contain more useful state than will fit in one model invocation.

Current production agent systems increasingly separate the durable session from the model's immediate context. Anthropic's Managed Agents architecture explicitly describes a session as broader than the context window and warns that irreversible compaction can lose information needed by future turns. Their long-running-agent guidance similarly relies on external artifacts and persistent state to bridge context boundaries.

This distinction yields a useful model:

```text
                 Agent memory system
                        │
        ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
        │               │                │
        ▼               ▼                ▼
  Durable history   Structured state   Knowledge stores
        │               │                │
        └───────────────┼────────────────┘
                        ▼
                 retrieval / selection
                        │
                        ▼
                   active context
```

The model should not need every remembered item in active context at once.

sections.heading: 3.1 Active context
3.2 Working memory
sections.text:
Explicit mutable state required to continue an ongoing task.

Examples:

```yaml
objective: Add refreshable IAM database authentication
phase: implementation
changed_files:
  - src/db/auth.ts
  - src/db/client.ts
open_failures:
  - integration test still uses static password fixture
decisions:
  - refresh credentials before opening a new connection
remaining:
  - update fixture
  - run lint
  - run typecheck
  - run integration tests
```

Working memory should be concise, structured where possible, and scoped to a task or workflow.

It normally expires when the task ends unless selected information is promoted elsewhere.

sections.heading: 3.3 Episodic memory
3.4 Semantic memory
3.5 Procedural memory
4. Memory Is Different From Source of Truth
sections.text:
Agents should not copy durable facts into memory when a stronger authoritative source already exists and can be queried cheaply.

For example:

```text
Weak design:
Memory says "package version is 4.2.1"

Preferred design:
Read package.json when the current version is needed
```

Likewise:

```text
Weak design:
Remember the current database schema indefinitely

Preferred design:
Use schema inspection + remember only durable architectural facts
```

Memory should reduce unnecessary rediscovery, not compete with authoritative state.

A useful ordering is:

```text
authoritative live source
        >
versioned organization/scope/repository knowledge
        >
promoted semantic memory
        >
episodic recollection
        >
model inference
```

This is not an instruction-authority hierarchy; it is a **factual reliability heuristic** and must still account for freshness and provenance.

sections.heading: 5. Memory Promotion
sections.text:
Not everything an agent observes should become durable memory.

the platform should use an explicit promotion lifecycle:

```text
observation
   ↓
working state
   ↓
validated candidate memory
   ↓
semantic / procedural promotion
   ↓
review / expiry / supersession
```

sections.heading: Automatically retainable state
Candidate memory
sections.text:
Potentially reusable information can be stored as a candidate rather than immediately treated as truth.

Example:

```yaml
claim: "This repository uses pnpm for package management."
status: candidate
source:
  type: repository-file
  path: package.json
observed_at: 2026-09-30
confidence: high
```

A later validation or deterministic extraction process can promote it.

sections.heading: Durable semantic knowledge
6. What Should Not Be Learned Automatically
7. Provenance-Aware Memory
sections.text:
Every durable memory item should answer:

```text
What is this?
Where did it come from?
When was it observed?
Who or what created it?
What scope does it apply to?
How was it validated?
What evidence supports it?
When should it be rechecked?
What supersedes it?
```

A conceptual record might look like:

```yaml
id: MEM-REPO-00421
type: semantic
scope:
  organization: project-a
  repository: customer-platform
claim: "Production deployments require approval from the release workflow."
source:
  kind: repository
  path: .github/workflows/release.yml
  revision: 81ac19b
observed_at: 2026-09-30T18:00:00Z
validation:
  method: deterministic-extraction
status: active
review_after: 2026-12-30
```

This is substantially safer than an unstructured vector-memory entry such as:

> Project A requires approval for production.

sections.heading: 8. Scope Is Mandatory
sections.text:
Memory without scope becomes contamination.

At minimum, a memory system may need to distinguish:

```text
public/general
the enterprise
client
project
repository
branch/environment
task/session
user
```

A repository convention learned from Project A must not appear in Project B's context.

A temporary feature-branch fact should not become repository-wide truth.

A development-environment workaround should not silently become a production standard.

sections.heading: 9. Temporal Semantics and Freshness
10. Contradiction Is Normal
sections.text:
Persistent systems will eventually encounter conflicting information.

A memory architecture should preserve contradiction rather than overwrite history silently.

Example:

```text
2026-01: Node 20 required
2026-08: Node 22 required
```

The correct representation is not necessarily deletion of the first observation. It may be:

```text
old fact → superseded
new fact → active
```

This allows the system to answer both:

> What is required now?

and

> Why did this historical build use Node 20?

sections.heading: 11. Retention and Forgetting
sections.text:
A memory system requires deletion and expiry semantics, not just insertion.

Possible retention policies include:

sections.heading: Task-scoped
sections.text: Delete or archive after task completion.

sections.heading: Session-scoped
sections.text: Retain only for the active agent session.

sections.heading: Time-limited
sections.text: Expire after a defined interval unless refreshed.

sections.heading: Source-bound
sections.text: Remain valid while a source revision or external record remains authoritative.

sections.heading: Reviewed durable
sections.text: Persist indefinitely but undergo periodic validation.

sections.heading: Event-sourced
sections.text:
Retain immutable history while separately maintaining current effective state.

the platform should avoid indefinite retention by default where no continuing value exists.

sections.heading: 12. Memory Retrieval
13. Episodic vs Semantic Retrieval
sections.text:
These answer different questions.

Semantic memory:

> What do we currently know about this repository?

Episodic memory:

> What happened the last three times this deployment failed?

Collapsing both into the same flat vector store can make temporal and causal reasoning harder.

Recent research on long-horizon agents increasingly explores layered episodic/semantic designs rather than relying on one universal memory representation. These results are promising but should be treated as external evidence rather than an the platform standard until reproduced against engineering workloads.

sections.heading: 14. Procedural Memory Should Prefer Explicit Artifacts
sections.text:
When an agent learns a better way to perform recurring work, the platform should prefer promotion into:

```text
skill
playbook
script
standard
pattern
ADR
experiment result
```

rather than allowing an opaque memory store to become the only place where the procedure exists.

Example:

```text
Observed repeatedly:
"Running schema validation before generated-code checks avoids misleading failures."

Bad outcome:
Agent silently remembers this forever.

Preferred outcome:
Candidate insight
    ↓
validation
    ↓
update GraphQL skill/playbook
    ↓
version + eval
```

This turns experience into organizational knowledge that humans can inspect and other agents can reuse.

sections.heading: 15. Memory Writes Are Mutations
sections.text:
Memory insertion is a state-changing action.

That means persistent-memory writes deserve the same architectural scrutiny as other mutations.

Questions include:

- Does this agent have authority to write this scope?
- Can untrusted input cause durable memory poisoning?
- Is the write reversible?
- Is there an audit record?
- Can the memory be reviewed or deleted?
- Is provenance preserved?

Systems should not expose unrestricted `memory.write(anything)` capabilities to agents that process untrusted content.

sections.heading: 16. Memory Poisoning
17. Memory and Permission Isolation
sections.text:
multi-scope enterprise environments make isolation especially important.

the platform should assume that a future memory service may contain knowledge from many permission scopes.

Therefore:

> Authorization filtering must occur before relevance ranking.

The retrieval system should never retrieve all semantically similar memories and then attempt to remove unauthorized entries afterward.

Project, repository, and user scopes should be enforced at the storage/query boundary where practical.

sections.heading: 18. Memory and Privacy
19. Recommended platform Architecture
sections.text:
For long-running software-development agents, the current recommended conceptual architecture is:

```text
                    ┌──────────────────┐
                    │ Authoritative    │
                    │ external state   │
                    └────────┬─────────┘
                             │
                             ▼
┌───────────────┐    ┌───────────────┐
│ Episodic log  │    │ Semantic KB   │
│ / trace       │    │ / handbook    │
└───────┬───────┘    └───────┬───────┘
        │                    │
        ├──────────┬─────────┘
        │          │
        ▼          ▼
   memory retrieval / resolution
                │
                ▼
       structured working state
                │
                ▼
          active context
                │
                ▼
              agent
                │
                ▼
        tools / environment
                │
                └──── observations ────► episodic log
```

Candidate semantic/procedural memories should pass through a promotion path rather than being written directly from arbitrary observations.

sections.heading: 20. Memory Promotion Policy by Risk
sections.text: A practical starting model:

sections.heading: Low-risk automatic
Automatic with deterministic evidence
Review or stronger validation recommended
Human approval expected
21. Memory Quality Metrics
sections.text:
Memory systems should be evaluated on more than retrieval recall.

Useful metrics include:

sections.heading: Accuracy
sections.text: Is the retrieved memory correct?

sections.heading: Provenance fidelity
sections.text: Can the memory be traced to its evidence?

sections.heading: Freshness
sections.text: Does retrieval favor currently valid knowledge?

sections.heading: Scope precision
sections.text: Does memory remain within the correct scope/repository/task boundary?

sections.heading: Contradiction handling
sections.text: Does the system identify superseded or conflicting memories correctly?

sections.heading: False-memory rate
sections.text: How often does generated or inferred information become incorrectly stored as fact?

sections.heading: Retrieval usefulness
sections.text: Does the memory improve downstream task success?

sections.heading: Token efficiency
sections.text: How much active context is consumed per useful memory retrieval?

sections.heading: Write precision
sections.text: How many stored memories were actually worth retaining?

sections.heading: Deletion correctness
sections.text: Can expired or requested-for-removal information be reliably excluded?

sections.heading: EXP-CTX-024 — Automatic vs Gated Memory Promotion
EXP-CTX-025 — Flat Memory Store vs Layered Episodic/Semantic Memory
EXP-CTX-026 — Freshness- and Scope-Aware Memory Ranking
sections.text:
**Question:** Does explicitly incorporating temporal validity and scope into ranking reduce stale or cross-scope retrieval without harming useful recall?

Compare:

```text
semantic similarity only
vs
semantic + metadata filters
vs
semantic + scope + freshness-aware ranking
```

sections.heading: Recommended
sections.text:
- Separate active context, working state, episodic memory, semantic memory, and procedural knowledge.
- Preserve durable history outside the model context for recoverability.
- Prefer authoritative live sources over copied memories when inexpensive to query.
- Use structured working state for ongoing tasks.
- Preserve provenance for durable memory.
- Scope all persistent memory.
- Represent temporal validity and supersession where facts can change.
- Treat memory writes as privileged mutations.
- Separate candidate memories from approved organizational knowledge.
- Prefer explicit skills/playbooks/standards for durable procedural knowledge.
- Enforce authorization before memory retrieval/ranking.

sections.heading: Provisional
sections.text:
- Use layered episodic + semantic stores for complex long-running agents.
- Include freshness directly in memory ranking.
- Automate promotion when claims can be validated deterministically.

sections.heading: Not currently recommended
sections.text:
- A single unscoped vector database as the entire memory system.
- Automatically treating model-generated summaries as durable fact.
- Permanent retention of every interaction.
- Allowing untrusted content to write persistent procedural instructions.
- Using memory as a substitute for querying authoritative live state.
- Silent overwrite of contradictory historical facts.

sections.heading: 24. Relationship to the the platform Handbook
sections.text:
The handbook itself is a form of curated semantic and procedural organizational memory.

This makes it intentionally different from an autonomous memory store.

Handbook knowledge is:

- versioned;
- reviewed;
- typed;
- evidence-linked;
- explicitly scoped;
- promoted deliberately.

A future the platform memory service should be capable of surfacing candidate insights from operational experience, but the path should be:

```text
agent experience
    ↓
candidate insight
    ↓
evidence / experiment / review
    ↓
handbook or skill update
```

not:

```text
agent once believed something
    ↓
enterprise standard
```

sections.heading: 26. Conclusion
sections.text:
Memory is valuable when it reduces repeated discovery and preserves continuity. It becomes dangerous when transient observations silently turn into durable truth.

the platform should therefore treat memory as a governed information system:

> **remember execution state freely within scope; promote durable knowledge deliberately; preserve provenance; prefer authoritative sources; and make forgetting a first-class operation.**

The objective is not to make an agent remember everything.

The objective is to make the right information recoverable, trustworthy, current, and available when needed.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text:
Coding agents rarely fail only because they cannot generate code. They also fail because they do not know **where to look, which relationships matter, which files are authoritative, which tests encode behavior, or which parts of a repository should remain untouched**.

Repository context engineering is therefore the discipline of helping an agent discover and reason about the structure, behavior, history, and constraints of a software repository without forcing the repository into a tool or framework it does not otherwise need.

The objective is not to maximize repository information presented to the model.

The objective is to expose the smallest set of repository signals necessary to make a correct change.

---

sections.heading: 2. Core principle: observe before prescribing
3. Repository intelligence is multi-source
sections.text:
No single repository representation is sufficient for every engineering task.

Useful sources include:

```text
Repository
   |
   +-- filesystem structure
   +-- package/build metadata
   +-- exact text
   +-- symbols and types
   +-- references and call relationships
   +-- dependency graph
   +-- build/test graph
   +-- semantic index
   +-- repository map
   +-- tests
   +-- runtime/configuration
   +-- git history
   +-- ownership/review metadata
   +-- generated artifacts
   +-- documentation and ADRs
```

These signals should be treated as complementary rather than competing sources.

---

sections.heading: 4. Repository size should influence strategy
sections.text: A five-file project and a five-hundred-thousand-file monorepo should not receive the same context architecture.

sections.heading: Small repositories
Medium repositories
Large repositories
5. Prefer live authoritative signals where practical
6. Filesystem structure
sections.text:
Directory and file structure provide low-cost orientation.

Agents should usually be able to answer basic questions such as:

- Is this a single-package or multi-package repository?
- Where are source files located?
- Where are tests located?
- Which directories are generated?
- Are there separate frontend/backend packages?
- Are schemas, migrations, infrastructure, and documentation colocated or separated?

Filesystem structure should normally be discovered rather than permanently copied into global instructions.

Large directory trees should be filtered to avoid generated directories, dependencies, caches, binaries, coverage output, and other low-value material.

---

sections.heading: 7. Package, workspace, and build metadata
Example
sections.text:
In an existing Nx repository, an agent might use:

```text
list projects
   -> inspect project metadata
   -> inspect dependency graph
   -> identify relevant target
```

In a standalone React application, the equivalent orientation may simply be:

```text
package.json
   + src tree
   + tsconfig
   + bundler configuration
   + tests
```

Both approaches satisfy the same architectural goal: understand the repository using the structures already available.

---

sections.heading: 8. Exact search remains essential
9. Symbol-aware navigation
10. AST and structural analysis
11. Repository maps
sections.text:
A repository map is a compact representation of important files, symbols, and relationships intended to orient an agent before deeper inspection.

A repository map may contain:

```text
src/api/order.ts
  createOrder(...)
  cancelOrder(...)
      |
      +--> OrderService

src/services/order-service.ts
  OrderService
      |
      +--> OrderRepository
      +--> PaymentGateway

src/repositories/order-repository.ts
  OrderRepository
```

Repo maps can be generated using symbol extraction and graph ranking techniques or produced from existing build/dependency metadata.

sections.heading: Benefits
Risks
the platform position
sections.text:
Repository maps are a useful technique, not a universal requirement.

They should be evaluated against simpler repository-search mechanisms for the target workload.

Related experiment: `EXP-CTX-006`.

---

sections.heading: 12. Semantic repository retrieval
sections.text:
Semantic indexes are useful when task language and repository terminology differ.

Example:

> "Where do we prevent users from accessing another tenant's records?"

The relevant implementation may contain terms such as:

```text
organizationId
scopePredicate
resourceOwner
authorizationGuard
```

without containing the phrase "another tenant."

Semantic retrieval can bridge this vocabulary gap.

However, semantic similarity should not replace exact search, symbol navigation, or verification.

---

sections.heading: 13. Agent-directed exploration
sections.text:
A capable coding agent can iteratively navigate a repository using tools:

```text
inspect structure
   ↓
search
   ↓
read candidate
   ↓
follow symbol/reference
   ↓
inspect tests
   ↓
inspect configuration
   ↓
form hypothesis
   ↓
verify
```

This resembles how a developer investigates unfamiliar code.

Agent-directed exploration has several advantages:

- naturally adapts to unusual repositories;
- requires less precomputation;
- follows clues dynamically;
- works even when indexes are incomplete.

But exploration also consumes model calls and context and can fail through poor search decisions.

Recent empirical work suggests that delegated deep-search workflows can underperform indexed semantic retrieval on some read-only repository question-answering workloads. This should caution against assuming that autonomous exploration is inherently superior to indexing.

the platform should therefore evaluate **indexed retrieval and agentic exploration as complementary mechanisms**.

---

sections.heading: 14. Tests are repository intelligence
15. Git history as context
16. Ownership and organizational context
17. Runtime and operational signals
18. Generated code and artifacts
19. Context packs
sections.text:
For complex changes, repository discovery may produce a bounded **context pack**.

Example:

```text
Task: change order cancellation behavior

Relevant implementation:
- src/services/order-service.ts

Callers:
- src/api/order.ts
- src/jobs/order-timeout.ts

Tests:
- test/order-service.spec.ts

Configuration:
- config/order-policy.ts

Related decision:
- docs/adr/014-order-state-machine.md
```

The context pack should be a retrieval result, not a permanent repository description.

It should preserve citations or file paths so the agent can reopen authoritative sources when needed.

---

sections.heading: 20. Suggested repository discovery pipeline
sections.text:
A general-purpose coding-agent flow should look approximately like:

```text
1. Inspect repository shape
       ↓
2. Detect existing tooling and language ecosystem
       ↓
3. Identify exact clues from task
       ↓
4. Run cheap lexical/file/symbol discovery
       ↓
5. Add semantic/structural retrieval if needed
       ↓
6. Inspect relevant implementation
       ↓
7. Follow references/dependencies
       ↓
8. Inspect tests and constraints
       ↓
9. Build bounded working context
       ↓
10. Implement
       ↓
11. Verify using repository-native tooling
```

This sequence is intentionally adaptive.

Steps may be skipped when unnecessary.

---

sections.heading: 21. Tool-specific adapters
sections.text:
the platform should define abstract repository capabilities before defining vendor-specific implementations.

Example capabilities:

```text
repository.listFiles()
repository.searchText()
repository.findSymbol()
repository.findReferences()
repository.getDependencies()
repository.getBuildTargets()
repository.getTests()
repository.getDiff()
repository.getHistory()
```

Adapters may then implement those capabilities through the environment already present.

Examples:

```text
Nx              -> project/dependency/build graph
pnpm workspaces -> package relationships
Turborepo       -> task relationships
Bazel           -> target/build graph
TypeScript      -> type/symbol graph
LSP             -> definitions/references
Git             -> history/diff/ownership evidence
filesystem      -> universal fallback
```

This keeps handbook guidance portable while still allowing deep integration with capable tooling.

---

sections.heading: 22. Repository instructions versus repository intelligence
sections.text:
Repository instructions answer:

> How should work be performed here?

Repository intelligence answers:

> What exists here, and how is it connected?

These are different forms of context.

For example:

```text
AGENTS.md:
  Run integration tests before modifying API contracts.

Repository intelligence:
  API contracts live in packages/contracts.
  The relevant integration suite is test/api-contracts.
```

Instructions should not become a manually maintained duplicate of discoverable repository structure.

---

sections.heading: 23.1 Whole-repository ingestion
sections.text:
Loading large portions of a repository because context capacity permits it.

**Risk:** noise, cost, stale reasoning, lost attention.

sections.heading: 23.2 Tool-driven architecture distortion
sections.text:
Changing repository architecture primarily to make agent tooling easier.

**Risk:** unnecessary infrastructure and long-term maintenance burden.

sections.heading: 23.3 Stale index confidence
sections.text:
Treating precomputed indexes as authoritative after repository changes.

**Risk:** missed files and incorrect relationships.

sections.heading: 23.4 Semantic-only search
sections.text:
Using embeddings for identifiers and exact technical strings.

**Risk:** weak recall for precise code clues.

sections.heading: 23.5 Grep-only exploration
sections.text:
Treating string matches as sufficient understanding.

**Risk:** missing indirect semantic or structural relationships.

sections.heading: 23.6 Ignoring tests during discovery
sections.text: Reading implementation but not behavior specifications encoded in tests.

sections.heading: 23.7 Ignoring generated-content noise
sections.text: Allowing dependency folders or generated output to dominate search results.

sections.heading: 23.8 Framework assumption leakage
AEP-CTX-010-G1 — Inspect before prescribing
sections.text:
Repository tooling should be discovered before architecture recommendations are made.

**Status:** Approved

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-010-G2 — Use multiple repository signals
sections.text:
Code intelligence should combine exact, structural, semantic, behavioral, and historical signals as appropriate to the task.

**Status:** Recommended

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-010-G3 — Prefer authoritative live state for volatile facts
sections.text:
Use live filesystem, compiler, test, diff, and repository-native metadata where practical.

**Status:** Recommended

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-010-G4 — Treat indexes as acceleration structures
sections.text:
Precomputed indexes and maps accelerate discovery but should not silently become authoritative replacements for the current repository.

**Status:** Recommended

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-010-G5 — Tests belong in context acquisition
sections.text:
For behavior-changing work, relevant tests should usually be identified before implementation rather than only after it.

**Status:** Recommended

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-010-G6 — Repository maps are optional
sections.text:
Use repository maps when they measurably improve orientation or context efficiency.

**Status:** Provisional

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-010-G7 — Adapt strategy to repository scale and workload
sections.text:
Small repositories may require little or no indexing; large repositories may justify specialized indexes and graph representations.

**Status:** Recommended

sections.heading: Visual Studio Code — How Copilot understands your workspace
sections.text:
Current documentation describes coding agents combining semantic search, text search, grep, file search, symbol usages, directory listing, and direct file reading. It also notes that small repositories may be read more directly while larger repositories require selective search, and recommends excluding generated/noisy paths to reduce irrelevant context.

https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/reference/workspace-context

sections.heading: Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code Question Answering (2026)
sections.text:
The SWE-QA study compared indexed semantic search with delegated deep agentic search for repository-level question answering. On its evaluated workload, semantic search achieved higher answer accuracy and lower cost, while delegated search introduced substantial handoff failures. The result should not be generalized to every coding task, but it provides evidence against assuming agentic exploration always dominates indexing.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01507

sections.text:

https://agentpatternscatalog.github.io/patterns/patterns/repo-map-context.html

sections.text:
Reinforces the broader context-engineering principle that scaffolding and repository instructions should be periodically simplified as model capability improves rather than accumulating indefinitely.

https://developers.openai.com/blog/rethinking-skills-and-prompts-for-gpt-6-astra

sections.heading: 28. Conclusion
sections.text:
Repository context should be constructed from the repository that actually exists.

the platform should not standardize on a monorepo framework, vector database, repository map, semantic index, or code graph simply because those tools are useful in some environments.

Instead, coding agents should begin by observing:

```text
What is this repository?
What structure already exists?
What information does this task require?
What is the cheapest reliable way to obtain it?
```

The resulting architecture may be extremely simple for a small project and sophisticated for a large enterprise codebase.

Both can be correct.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text:
Agent systems often resend substantial portions of the same context across repeated model calls: system instructions, tool definitions, repository guidance, shared reference material, conversation history, or large source artifacts. Provider-side context caching can reduce the cost and latency of repeatedly processing those inputs.

Caching changes the economics of context, but it does **not** change the semantics of context.

A cached token still occupies model context. Irrelevant cached material can still distract the model, compete with task-relevant evidence, increase effective context complexity, and complicate invalidation.

the platform therefore treats context caching as a **performance optimization layered on top of good context engineering**, not as a substitute for selective context construction.

The primary objective is:

> **Reuse stable, relevant context economically without allowing cache behavior to determine what the model should know.**

---

sections.heading: 2. Caching and context quality are separate concerns
sections.text:
Two questions must be answered independently:

1. **Should this information be in active context?**
2. **If it is in active context repeatedly, can processing it be reused?**

The first is a context-engineering decision.

The second is a caching decision.

A useful rule is:

> **Relevance decides inclusion. Reuse decides caching.**

This prevents an attractive cache-hit rate from becoming a reason to preserve unnecessary context.

Bad reasoning:

```text
This 20K-token policy/reference block is cheap because it is cached,
therefore we should keep sending it.
```

Better reasoning:

```text
The agent needs 3K tokens from that material for this class of task.
Those 3K tokens are stable across many calls, so make that portion cache-friendly.
```

---

sections.heading: 3. What context caching usually means
sections.text:
Modern provider-side prompt/context caching generally avoids recomputing model state for repeated input prefixes or explicitly cached content.

The exact implementation, billing model, minimum size, retention period, and API controls vary by provider and model.

As of this baseline:

- OpenAI supports prompt-prefix caching on supported models, including explicit cache breakpoints on GPT-5.6-and-later model families; reuse depends on matching rendered prefixes and model/runtime settings.
- Google Gemini supports implicit prefix caching on current model families and explicit cached-content objects in APIs that expose them.
- Other model providers expose related mechanisms with different semantics, TTLs, pricing, and placement rules.

the platform should therefore model caching conceptually and isolate provider-specific behavior in adapters.

---

sections.heading: 4. Cacheable context classes
sections.text:
Candidate reusable context commonly includes:

```text
stable provider/application instructions
          |
organization standards
          |
repository bootstrap guidance
          |
stable tool definitions
          |
shared reference material
          |
conversation/session history
          |
large immutable artifacts
```

Not all of these should be cached in the same way.

sections.heading: 4.1 Stable instructions
4.2 Tool definitions
sections.text:
Tool schemas can consume significant context in agent systems with broad capabilities.

If the same tools remain exposed across repeated calls, stable tool definitions can benefit from caching.

However, AEP-CTX-007 still applies: a large tool catalog should not remain permanently active solely for caching convenience.

Dynamic tool discovery may reduce total context enough to outperform a highly cacheable but unnecessarily large catalog.

sections.heading: 4.3 Shared reference material
4.4 Session history
sections.text:
Append-only conversations can produce naturally reusable prefixes.

This can make long sessions cheaper when earlier turns remain unchanged.

Compaction, rewriting, or replacing history can reduce cache reuse even when it improves overall context quality. These effects should be evaluated together rather than optimizing one metric in isolation.

---

sections.heading: 5. Stable-prefix design
sections.text:
Prefix-oriented caches reward stable ordering.

A generic context layout might be:

```text
[ stable governing instructions ]
[ stable tool definitions       ]
[ stable shared references      ]
---------------- cache boundary --
[ scope/repository dynamic     ]
[ retrieved task context        ]
[ current task/request          ]
[ recent tool outputs           ]
```

This is a useful starting model, not a universal prescription.

The correct layout depends on:

- provider semantics;
- model family;
- whether tools are dynamically loaded;
- whether conversation history is append-only;
- whether shared references are actually relevant;
- privacy and isolation requirements;
- expected reuse frequency.

---

sections.heading: 6. Stability is an architectural property
7. Do not optimize for cache-hit percentage alone
8. Cache-write economics matter
9. Cache lifetime and workload shape
sections.text:
Cache usefulness depends heavily on request locality.

A stable prefix reused twenty times in ten minutes may be highly valuable.

The same prefix reused once per week may provide little benefit if provider cache retention is measured in minutes or hours.

Useful workload dimensions include:

```text
reuse frequency
reuse interval
prefix size
prefix volatility
parallel session count
model affinity
scope/workspace isolation
```

Caching should therefore be evaluated against realistic traffic rather than synthetic back-to-back calls alone.

---

sections.heading: 10. Explicit vs implicit caching
sections.text: Providers increasingly expose both implicit and explicit caching patterns.

sections.heading: Implicit caching
Explicit caching
11. Caching and progressive disclosure
sections.text:
Caching and progressive disclosure solve different problems.

Progressive disclosure asks:

> What should be loaded now?

Caching asks:

> If we load it repeatedly, can we avoid recomputing it?

They should complement each other.

Example:

```text
Always active
  small governing policy

Discoverable
  skill catalog metadata

Loaded on demand
  selected skill instructions

Retrieved
  relevant references

Cached when reused
  stable portions of the above
```

A well-designed system may have **less total cached content** than a poorly designed system because it avoids repeatedly loading unnecessary information.

---

sections.heading: 12. Caching and dynamic tool loading
sections.text:
Tool definitions are often part of the cacheable prompt prefix.

This creates a tension:

```text
stable full tool catalog
        -> potentially high cache reuse
        -> higher active-context footprint

selectively loaded tools
        -> lower active-context footprint
        -> changing suffix/catalog composition
```

Neither is universally better.

For a small stable toolset, keeping definitions fixed may be efficient.

For hundreds of tools, dynamic discovery can materially reduce context pressure even if it complicates prefix reuse.

The decision should be based on end-to-end performance.

This should eventually be evaluated jointly with EXP-CTX-020.

---

sections.heading: 13. Caching and compaction
sections.text:
Compaction can invalidate part of a reusable conversation prefix.

That does not mean compaction is bad.

For example:

```text
Before compaction:
50K tokens
40K cached

After compaction:
12K tokens
0K cached initially
```

The post-compaction call may temporarily lose cache savings while still being much cheaper and cognitively cleaner overall.

Therefore:

> **Never retain bloated history solely to preserve a cache hit.**

Compaction and caching should be evaluated using total task cost and success across the entire workflow.

---

sections.heading: 14. Caching and retrieval
sections.text:
Retrieval and caching can also complement each other.

Repeated tasks may retrieve the same stable documents.

Possible strategies include:

```text
retrieve every time
        |
retrieve + cache common selected context
        |
cache stable base + retrieve changing evidence
```

However, caching retrieved knowledge introduces freshness concerns.

If the underlying source can change, the application must understand what causes invalidation.

This is particularly important for:

- repository files;
- active API documentation;
- scoped policies;
- tickets/issues;
- database state;
- operational runbooks.

A cache must never silently become a stale source of truth.

---

sections.heading: 15. Cache invalidation
16. Authorization and tenant isolation
sections.text:
Cache reuse must never violate isolation boundaries.

Provider-managed caches typically provide organization/project-level isolation semantics, but the platform systems still need explicit application-level scope discipline.

Do not optimize shared cache reuse across permission scopes if doing so creates ambiguity about data ownership, authorization, billing, or side-channel exposure.

Useful cache scopes may include:

```text
organization
client
workspace
repository
user
session
```

The correct scope depends on the sensitivity and ownership of the content.

When in doubt, prefer narrower reuse over cross-boundary optimization.

---

sections.heading: 17. Privacy and retention
sections.text:
Caching can have data-retention implications distinct from ordinary inference.

Provider behavior differs substantially:

- some caches are ephemeral in-memory state;
- some providers expose extended cache retention;
- explicit cached-content systems may persist content for a configured TTL;
- enterprise/ZDR rules may alter what is allowed.

Therefore:

> **Caching configuration is part of the data-governance architecture.**

Before enabling explicit or extended retention for scoped data, verify current provider documentation, contractual terms, organizational settings, and the sensitivity classification of the content.

Provider caching behavior is volatile guidance and should be reviewed frequently.

---

sections.heading: 18. Prewarming
19. Cache-aware context construction
sections.text:
A practical context builder should conceptually classify context along at least two independent axes:

```text
Relevance / necessity

required
useful
optional
irrelevant

        x

Stability / reuse

stable
semi-stable
volatile
one-shot
```

This produces better decisions than a single `cacheable: true/false` flag.

Example:

| Context item | Relevance | Stability | Likely treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Core safety policy | required | stable | active + cache-friendly |
| Repository language/version | required | semi-stable | active; versioned |
| Complete engineering handbook | low for most tasks | stable | retrieve selectively; do not preload |
| Current test failure | required | volatile | active, uncached suffix |
| Selected skill instructions | useful/required | stable | load on demand; cache if reused |
| Current git diff | required | volatile | active, refresh live |

---

sections.heading: 20. Cache-aware layout should remain provider-portable
21.1 Cache-driven context bloat
sections.text:
**Failure:** Content remains active because it is inexpensive to cache.

**Consequence:** Lower context quality despite attractive billing metrics.

**Mitigation:** Apply relevance filtering before cache optimization.

sections.heading: 21.2 Volatile prefixes
sections.text:
**Failure:** Timestamps, randomized ordering, dynamic IDs, or task-specific text appear before otherwise stable material.

**Consequence:** Poor cache reuse.

**Mitigation:** Separate stable and dynamic context structurally.

sections.heading: 21.3 Cache-hit vanity metrics
sections.text:
**Failure:** Teams optimize hit percentage rather than total task economics.

**Consequence:** Local optimization can increase total cost or reduce quality.

**Mitigation:** Measure full workflow cost, latency, and success.

sections.heading: 21.4 Stale cached evidence
sections.text:
**Failure:** Cached repository/scope/reference content survives source changes.

**Consequence:** Agent reasons from obsolete state.

**Mitigation:** Version and invalidate mutable knowledge; prefer live authoritative reads for volatile facts.

sections.heading: 21.5 Cross-scope reuse
sections.text:
**Failure:** Caches unintentionally span consumers/users/security scopes.

**Consequence:** Privacy, billing, or information-leak risks.

**Mitigation:** Scope caches explicitly and follow provider isolation guidance.

sections.heading: 21.6 Overengineering explicit caching
sections.text:
**Failure:** Application code gains complex cache lifecycle logic before reuse patterns are understood.

**Consequence:** Operational complexity exceeds savings.

**Mitigation:** Start with provider defaults and add explicit controls only after measurement.

sections.heading: 21.7 Preserving history solely for cache reuse
sections.text:
**Failure:** Compaction is delayed to avoid invalidating cached prefixes.

**Consequence:** Context becomes bloated or semantically noisy.

**Mitigation:** Prioritize context quality and total workflow economics.

---

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-011-G1 — Cache only after relevance selection
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Context should first earn inclusion in active context. Cacheability is a secondary optimization.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-011-G2 — Put stable reusable context before volatile context where provider semantics reward prefix stability
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Do not allow timestamps, random ordering, or task-specific material to unnecessarily fragment reusable prefixes.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-011-G3 — Keep stable structures deterministic
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Tool definitions, policy blocks, and shared reference ordering should be deterministic when their semantics are unchanged.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-011-G4 — Measure total workflow economics
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Track cache reads/writes or storage, total input, latency, task quality, and invalidation behavior—not only hit rate.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-011-G5 — Prefer implicit caching before custom lifecycle machinery
sections.text:
**Status:** Provisional

Where provider-managed caching is available, begin there unless explicit caching solves a measured problem.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-011-G6 — Do not preserve irrelevant history for cache reuse
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Compaction and context reduction remain valid even when they temporarily reduce cache hits.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-011-G7 — Treat explicit cache retention as data governance
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Cache lifetime and storage semantics must comply with scope and enterprise data requirements.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-011-G8 — Scope caches no more broadly than required
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Cost optimization must not weaken tenant, repository, user, or authorization boundaries.

sections.heading: AEP-CTX-011-G9 — Keep cache semantics behind provider adapters
sections.text:
**Status:** Recommended

Handbook and application architecture should remain portable across changing vendor APIs.

---

sections.text:
This chapter adds the following questions to the central research register:

- Q-CACHE-002 — How should cache-friendly layout interact with progressive disclosure and dynamic tool loading?
- Q-CACHE-003 — When does explicit caching outperform provider-managed implicit caching after operational complexity is included?
- Q-CACHE-004 — What cache invalidation keys are required for repository and project knowledge?
- Q-CACHE-005 — How should compaction thresholds change when large portions of conversation history are cached?
