sections.heading: EXP-CTX-009 — Cache-Aware Context Layout
EXP-CTX-029 — Progressive Disclosure vs Cache-Optimized Static Prefix
EXP-CTX-030 — Explicit vs Implicit Caching
EXP-CTX-031 — Cache-Aware Compaction
25. Recommended instrumentation
sections.text:
Agent traces should record caching information when the provider exposes it.

Suggested normalized fields:

```yaml
cache:
  provider: openai
  mode: implicit
  scope: repository-session
  input_tokens: 18000
  cached_read_tokens: 12000
  cache_write_tokens: 0
  estimated_cache_cost: null
  ttl_seconds: null
  context_version: repo-guidance-v12
```

Provider adapters can populate only supported fields.

At the aggregate level, track:

- cache-eligible tokens;
- cache-read ratio;
- cache-write frequency;
- net token cost;
- latency savings;
- invalidations;
- task-success correlation.

---

sections.heading: 26. Relationship to future the platform MCP
sections.text:
The future handbook MCP should not simply return a large stable block because that block happens to cache well.

Instead:

```text
request
   ↓
resolve applicable guidance
   ↓
retrieve smallest sufficient knowledge
   ↓
classify stable vs volatile
   ↓
construct provider-neutral context package
   ↓
provider adapter optimizes cache placement
```

This preserves the separation between:

- **knowledge selection**;
- **context construction**;
- **provider-specific inference optimization**.

That separation will make the system easier to test and substantially more portable.

---

sections.heading: 27. External evidence baseline
sections.text: The initial guidance in this chapter is informed by current provider documentation as of 2026-09-30.

sections.heading: OpenAI
sections.text:
OpenAI documents prefix-based prompt caching for supported models and recommends placing stable instructions and reference material before dynamic content, keeping tool definitions/order stable, and preserving append-only conversation history where appropriate. GPT-5.6-and-later models additionally expose explicit prompt-cache breakpoints and cache policy controls. OpenAI also documents that compaction can reduce cache reuse because it changes earlier context.

References:

- https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching
- https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/deployment-checklist

sections.heading: Google Gemini
sections.text:
Google documents implicit context caching for current Gemini model families and explicit cached-content objects in supported APIs. Its guidance similarly recommends placing large common content at the beginning of prompts for implicit reuse. Explicit caches introduce configurable TTL/storage semantics and are presented for recurring work over large repeated inputs, including repository analysis.

References:

- https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching
- https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/optimization

Provider-specific behavior is intentionally not promoted to a permanent the platform architectural requirement.

---

sections.heading: 28. Conclusion
sections.text:
Caching can materially improve agent cost and latency, especially when agents repeatedly process stable instructions, tools, references, or growing conversation prefixes.

But caching should remain subordinate to context quality.

The durable the platform principle is:

> **First minimize and structure the context the agent actually needs. Then make the reusable portion cheap.**

A system with excellent retrieval, progressive disclosure, compaction, and context selection may send fewer tokens even if its cache-hit rate is lower.

That is preferable to a highly cached system carrying large amounts of irrelevant context.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
2. Why a failure taxonomy matters
sections.text:
Agent behavior is often diagnosed at the wrong layer.

A developer may conclude that:

```text
"the model is bad at this task"
```

when the actual failure was:

```text
wrong file retrieved
      ↓
stale implementation loaded
      ↓
correct reasoning over incorrect evidence
```

or:

```text
relevant policy present
      ↓
80K tokens of competing context
      ↓
policy ignored or misapplied
```

or:

```text
untrusted README contains instructions
      ↓
agent interprets them as operating policy
      ↓
tool call exceeds intended authority
```

A useful taxonomy allows failures to be attributed to the system component that can actually fix them.

---

sections.heading: 3. Context failure model
sections.text:
the platform classifies context failures across six dimensions:

```text
Availability   — Was required information present?
Selection      — Was the right information selected?
Quality        — Was the information accurate and current?
Authority      — Was it allowed to influence behavior at that level?
Interpretation — Did the model understand and apply it correctly?
Lifecycle      — Was it retained, compacted, invalidated, or removed correctly?
```

These dimensions are intentionally separate.

For example, a retrieved document may be:

- relevant;
- accurate;
- recent;
- but untrusted as an instruction source.

Conversely, a enterprise standard may be:

- authoritative;
- trusted;
- but irrelevant to the current task.

---

sections.heading: 4. Failure Class: Under-Contexting
Mitigations
Evaluation signal
sections.text:
Measure whether relevant evidence was available to the agent before the incorrect decision occurred.

---

sections.heading: 5. Failure Class: Over-Contexting
Important distinction
sections.text:
```text
fits in context != useful in context
```

sections.heading: Mitigations
6. Failure Class: Context Dilution
sections.text:
Context dilution is a more specific form of over-contexting where high-value instructions or evidence are surrounded by large volumes of low-signal material.

Example:

```text
3 critical constraints
+
65 files
+
large test logs
+
full tool schemas
+
conversation history
```

The important information has not disappeared, but its effective salience may decline.

Mitigation should usually focus on increasing **signal density**, not merely rearranging prose.

Useful techniques include:

- structured state;
- concise task constraints;
- targeted evidence retrieval;
- summarized tool results with recoverable raw output;
- source-specific context sections.

---

sections.heading: 7. Failure Class: Stale Context
Required properties
sections.text:
Potentially volatile context should carry enough metadata to assess freshness where practical:

```yaml
source: repository
commit: abc123
retrieved_at: 2026-09-30T20:00:00-04:00
scope: packages/api
```

sections.heading: Mitigations
8. Failure Class: Contradictory Context
sections.text:
Agents commonly encounter multiple sources that disagree.

Examples:

```text
enterprise standard vs project standard
repository README vs current implementation
old ADR vs superseding ADR
user request vs safety boundary
retrieved documentation vs installed dependency version
```

A robust system should not rely on the model to silently infer precedence from prose order.

AEP-CTX-002 defines authority, trust, scope, and specificity as separate dimensions.

sections.heading: Preferred behavior
sections.text:
The system should attempt to resolve contradictions structurally.

If resolution is impossible, the conflict should remain explicit.

Bad behavior:

```text
choose whichever statement appeared last
```

Better behavior:

```text
Source A says X.
Source B says Y.
B is repository-specific and current, while A is general guidance.
Effective guidance: Y.
```

Where neither source dominates, human clarification may be appropriate.

---

sections.heading: 9. Failure Class: Authority Confusion
Rule
sections.text:
> **Relevance does not grant authority.**

A document may be the most relevant search result and still have zero authority to redefine system behavior.

---

sections.heading: 10. Failure Class: Context Poisoning
sections.text:
Context poisoning occurs when malicious, misleading, or corrupted content influences future decisions.

Prompt injection is one important form.

Other forms include:

- incorrect generated summaries;
- poisoned retrieval corpora;
- compromised documentation;
- malicious source comments;
- hallucinated facts written into durable memory;
- attacker-controlled tool output;
- manipulated external records.

The risk increases when poisoned content can persist beyond the current interaction.

```text
untrusted content
      ↓
agent accepts claim
      ↓
claim written to memory
      ↓
future sessions retrieve claim
      ↓
poison becomes durable
```

This is why AEP-CTX-009 treats durable memory writes as privileged mutations.

sections.heading: Mitigation strategy
11. Failure Class: Retrieval Flooding
Mitigations
12. Failure Class: Retrieval Blind Spots
13. Failure Class: Scope Leakage
sections.text:
Scope leakage occurs when context from one authority domain becomes visible or influential in another.

Examples:

```text
Project A guidance → Project B session
private repo context → unrelated project
user preference → organization policy
experimental finding → approved standard
production secrets → development agent
```

Scope leakage is both a correctness and security problem.

sections.heading: Mitigations
14. Failure Class: Compaction Drift
Preferred architecture
sections.text:
```text
durable raw history
        +
structured working state
        +
compact narrative context
```

Compaction should be recoverable whenever practical.

If an agent encounters uncertainty after compaction, it should be able to return to primary source material rather than treating the summary as infallible.

---

sections.heading: 15. Failure Class: Memory Contamination
Rule
sections.text:
> **A statement becoming memorable does not make it true.**

Durable memory should carry provenance, scope, freshness, confidence, and promotion status where those properties matter.

---

sections.heading: 16. Failure Class: Tool-Output Overload
Better pattern
sections.text:
```text
raw tool output
      ↓
structured parser / filter
      ↓
compact operational result
      ↓
agent context
```

while retaining the raw artifact for recovery when needed.

Examples:

```text
10,000-line test output
        ↓
failed tests + relevant stack traces + summary
```

or:

```text
entire dependency graph
        ↓
subgraph surrounding affected component
```

The summarizer itself should not become a hidden source of truth. Important raw evidence should remain recoverable.

---

sections.heading: 17. Failure Class: Context Echo
sections.text:
Context echo occurs when generated information is repeatedly fed back into the system as if independently verified.

Example:

```text
agent hypothesis
   ↓
summary
   ↓
memory
   ↓
retrieval result
   ↓
agent sees the same claim as supporting evidence
```

The result can resemble false consensus.

sections.heading: Mitigation
sections.text:
Provenance should distinguish:

```text
primary evidence
external source
human decision
model inference
model-generated summary
derived memory
```

Derived information should not silently gain evidentiary weight through repetition.

---

sections.heading: 18. Failure Class: Premature Context Commitment
sections.text:
An agent may lock onto an early interpretation and retrieve only evidence supporting it.

Example:

```text
initial guess: authentication bug
      ↓
retrieve auth files only
      ↓
ignore networking/configuration evidence
      ↓
reinforce original guess
```

This is a retrieval form of confirmation bias.

sections.heading: Mitigations
19. Failure Class: Instruction Bloat
Better response to a failure
sections.text:
Before adding another instruction, ask:

```text
Can a deterministic check prevent this?
Can a tool provide the missing evidence?
Should a skill own this guidance?
Is this rule still necessary with the current model?
Can an eval detect regression instead?
```

The handbook should periodically remove scaffolding that no longer produces measurable benefit.

---

sections.heading: 20. Failure Class: Cache-Driven Bloat
sections.text:
Context caching can make large stable prefixes economically attractive.

That creates a failure mode where unnecessary material is retained solely to maximize cache reuse.

AEP-CTX-011 establishes the governing rule:

> **Relevance decides inclusion. Reuse decides caching.**

Cached irrelevant context still consumes attention and context-window capacity.

---

sections.heading: 21. Failure Class: Hidden Transformation
sections.text:
Information often passes through transformations before reaching the model:

```text
source
  ↓
parser
  ↓
chunker
  ↓
metadata generation
  ↓
embedding
  ↓
retrieval
  ↓
reranking
  ↓
summarization
  ↓
context formatting
```

Any stage can distort or omit information.

Observability should therefore record enough of this pipeline to reconstruct why a piece of evidence was or was not presented.

At minimum, high-value retrieval systems should be able to answer:

```text
What source was queried?
Which candidates were retrieved?
Which were removed and why?
Which were reranked?
Which were shown to the model?
What transformations occurred?
```

---

sections.heading: 22. Failure Class: Provenance Loss
23. Failure Class: Authority Without Capability Boundaries
24. Failure Class: Silent Recovery Failure
sections.text:
Agents often recover from errors successfully, but a failed recovery can create misleading state.

Example:

```text
edit fails
   ↓
agent assumes edit succeeded
   ↓
subsequent reasoning depends on nonexistent change
```

Similar problems occur when:

- a tool result is truncated;
- a file read is partial;
- a retrieval service times out;
- a cache misses;
- an index is stale;
- a subagent fails silently.

Tool and retrieval failures should be represented explicitly rather than converted into plausible empty results.

---

sections.heading: 25. Detecting context failures
sections.text:
Many context failures are not visible from the final response alone.

Useful telemetry includes:

```text
active context size
context source breakdown
retrieved candidate count
selected candidate count
retrieval/rerank scores
source age
source scope
instruction conflicts
memory writes
compaction events
tool-output size
truncation events
cache metrics
tool authority
approval events
```

Trace-based analysis is therefore a core part of context debugging.

OpenAI's current agent guidance recommends trace graders and evals to inspect not only final answers but also tool calls and intermediate behavior.

---

sections.heading: 26. Context health metrics
sections.text:
No single metric captures context quality.

Potential metrics include:

sections.heading: Availability
sections.text:
- required-evidence recall;
- missing-context rate.

sections.heading: Precision
sections.text:
- fraction of active context judged relevant;
- duplicate-context rate.

sections.heading: Freshness
sections.text:
- stale-source rate;
- index/repository revision mismatch rate.

sections.heading: Authority
sections.text:
- unauthorized instruction-following rate;
- prompt-injection success rate.

sections.heading: Lifecycle
Efficiency
Outcome
27. Context failure response ladder
sections.text:
When an agent fails, debugging should move through a structured sequence.

```text
1. Was the required information available?
                 ↓
2. Was it retrieved or loaded?
                 ↓
3. Was it current and correct?
                 ↓
4. Was its authority represented correctly?
                 ↓
5. Was conflicting information resolved?
                 ↓
6. Was the active context overloaded?
                 ↓
7. Did compaction or memory alter it?
                 ↓
8. Did the model misinterpret correct context?
                 ↓
9. Did tool/capability boundaries limit damage?
```

Only after these questions should the failure automatically be attributed to model capability.

---

sections.heading: 28. Recommended platform failure taxonomy
sections.text:
For incident and eval labeling, use the following initial categories:

```text
CTX-AVAIL   missing required context
CTX-OVER    excessive context
CTX-DILUTE  low signal density
CTX-STALE   outdated context
CTX-CONFLICT contradictory context
CTX-AUTH    authority/trust confusion
CTX-POISON  malicious or corrupted context
CTX-FLOOD   retrieval flooding
CTX-BLIND   retrieval blind spot
CTX-SCOPE   scope leakage
CTX-COMPACT compaction drift
CTX-MEM     memory contamination
CTX-TOOL    tool-output overload or distortion
CTX-ECHO    generated evidence feedback loop
CTX-ANCHOR  premature context commitment
CTX-INSTR   instruction bloat
CTX-CACHE   cache-driven bloat
CTX-XFORM   transformation loss
CTX-PROV    provenance loss
CTX-RECOVER silent recovery failure
```

A failure may receive multiple labels.

Example:

```text
CTX-STALE + CTX-PROV
```

might identify a bug caused by outdated documentation whose version was not represented in retrieved context.

---

sections.heading: 29. Evaluation implications
EXP-CTX-032 — Distractor Density and Context Rot
EXP-CTX-033 — Raw vs Structured Tool Output
EXP-CTX-034 — Provenance and Freshness Labels
sections.text:
**Hypothesis:** Explicit source, scope, and freshness metadata will reduce stale-context and conflict-resolution failures in repositories containing deliberately contradictory historical material.

---

sections.heading: 31. Initial platform guidance
sections.text:
the platform currently recommends:

1. Treat context as typed, scoped information rather than undifferentiated text.
2. Preserve the distinction between relevance, trust, authority, freshness, and provenance.
3. Prefer the smallest sufficient active context, not the smallest possible context.
4. Keep raw source material recoverable when using lossy transformations.
5. Treat prompt injection as one member of a broader context-poisoning class.
6. Prevent untrusted content from gaining instructional authority through retrieval or placement.
7. Apply authorization and scope/repository isolation before relevance ranking.
8. Treat durable memory writes as privileged operations.
9. Explicitly detect stale indexes, stale memory, and version mismatches where feasible.
10. Summarize or structure large tool outputs before placing them in active context.
11. Avoid optimizing cache hit rate, retrieval recall, or context utilization independently of task success.
12. Record context transformations and retrieval decisions in traces where operationally reasonable.
13. Test systems against noisy, stale, conflicting, and adversarial context—not only ideal inputs.
14. Use deterministic capability boundaries so context failure does not automatically become operational compromise.
15. Diagnose context pipeline failures before concluding that a task requires a more capable model.

---

sections.heading: Strong external support
Recommended but requiring the platform validation
Experimental
34. Conclusion
sections.text:
Context engineering is not successful merely when the agent receives enough information.

A robust system must ensure that context is:

```text
available
relevant
current
properly scoped
correctly trusted
traceable
recoverable
and proportionate to the task
```

The practical goal is therefore not maximum context.

It is **controlled evidence flow**.

That principle will carry forward into later handbook sections on tools, MCP, agent architecture, memory, security, evaluation, and long-running execution.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Agent economics must be optimized around useful outcomes rather than isolated token or request prices. A system that is cheap per call but unreliable, slow, or dependent on frequent human repair may be more expensive in practice than a higher-priced configuration.

sections.heading: 2. Core objective
3. The performance budget
sections.text:
For a production workflow, define explicit budgets where practical:

```text
quality floor
cost ceiling
latency target
p95 latency target
human-intervention ceiling
retry ceiling
```

If the system cannot meet all targets, report the tradeoff rather than hiding it in averages.

sections.heading: 4. Optimization order
5. Local vs global optimization
6. Current recommendation
sections.text: Treat cost, latency, and reliability as first-class architectural properties from initial design through production operation. Every optimization must preserve or deliberately trade against an explicit quality objective.

sections.heading: 7. Living knowledge
sections.text: Pricing, model capability, cache behavior, rate limits, and infrastructure efficiency change quickly. Cost guidance must therefore be versioned, measured from real telemetry, and revalidated after relevant provider or architecture changes.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Agent systems have more cost centers than model tokens. Cost accounting should make the whole task economically visible.

sections.heading: 2. Cost taxonomy
sections.text: Track where material:

sections.heading: Model cost
Tool and infrastructure cost
Human cost
3. Required attribution
sections.text:
Costs should be attributable to useful dimensions such as:

```text
client
workspace/repository
workflow
task class
model/configuration
agent/subagent
tool
experiment/version
```

Avoid cross-scope accounting ambiguity.

sections.heading: 4. Unit economics
sections.text:
Useful normalized metrics include:

```text
cost / successful task
cost / merged change
cost / resolved incident
cost / accepted review finding
human minutes / accepted output
retry cost / task
wasted spend / abandoned trajectory
```

sections.heading: 5. Marginal cost
sections.text: When evaluating an added component, measure incremental value and incremental cost. A reranker, critic, subagent, or larger model must justify its marginal cost rather than merely improve a local metric.

sections.heading: 6. Cost attribution for shared infrastructure
sections.text:
Shared indexes, cached prompts, and persistent services should be accounted separately from marginal request cost. For enterprise engineering work, distinguish:

```text
fixed platform cost
+ shared operating cost
+ scope-specific marginal cost
```

sections.heading: 7. Recommendation
sections.text: Build cost accounting from traces and provider usage fields rather than estimates alone. Estimated prices are useful for planning, but production decisions should rely on realized cost per outcome.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Token reduction is valuable only when it removes low-value work without reducing task success.

sections.heading: 2. High-signal context first
3. Input vs output economics
sections.text: Input and output have different cost and latency characteristics. Long generated reasoning or verbose intermediate text can dominate cost even when input is efficient. Measure both.

sections.heading: 4. Context retention decisions
sections.text:
For every large context item ask:

```text
Is it relevant now?
Must it be active, or can it remain retrievable?
Is it reusable across turns?
Is the source authoritative and fresh?
Does removing it increase retries or errors?
```

sections.heading: 5. Tool-result reduction
sections.text: Prefer structured summaries and pointers for large tool results, while keeping raw evidence recoverable. Do not destroy information needed for debugging, security, or later verification merely to save tokens.

sections.heading: 6. Avoid token micro-optimization too early
sections.text: Current provider guidance notes that input-token trimming may have limited impact unless contexts are very large; reducing requests, outputs, or using appropriate models can dominate. Optimize measured bottlenecks first.

sections.heading: 7. Recommendation
sections.text: Evaluate context-efficiency changes against downstream success, retry rate, and cost per success—not token count in isolation.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Every model call, tool call, handoff, and coordination boundary adds latency, cost, and potential failure.

sections.heading: 2. Reduce unnecessary round trips
sections.text:
Where semantics are predictable, combine deterministic work rather than asking the model to orchestrate every micro-step.

Examples:

```text
filter + sort + aggregate in code
instead of
model -> tool -> model -> tool -> model
```

sections.heading: 3. Tool call economics
4. Multi-agent overhead
sections.text: Subagents can reduce wall time for independent work, but they also duplicate model context and synthesis cost. Account for all child-agent usage when comparing architectures.

sections.heading: 5. Fuse deterministic operations
sections.text: When a workflow always performs the same sequence, implement it as deterministic application code or a domain-coherent tool unless there is value in model-directed branching.

sections.heading: 6. Prefer one high-information call over many low-information calls
sections.text: Do not mechanically minimize calls if doing so creates overloaded prompts or brittle tools. The target is useful work per round trip.

sections.heading: 7. Recommendation
sections.text: Instrument request and tool graphs. Optimize repeated communication and redundant orchestration before tuning token-level details.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Users experience end-to-end delay, not token throughput. Optimize the critical path and perceived responsiveness rather than model latency alone.

sections.heading: 2. Decompose latency
sections.text:
Track:

```text
queue time
model time-to-first-token
model generation time
tool latency
network latency
sandbox startup
handoff/synthesis time
human approval time
```

sections.heading: 3. Tail latency
sections.text: p95/p99 behavior matters for agent systems because retries, slow tools, and long reasoning tails can create severe outliers. Report both median and tail latency.

sections.heading: 4. Interactive vs asynchronous classes
sections.text: Classify workloads before optimizing:

sections.heading: Interactive
sections.text: Prioritize responsiveness and progressive feedback.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Prioritize throughput and economics; batching/flex processing may be preferable.

sections.heading: Long-running agent task
sections.text: Expose durable progress and resumability rather than blocking a synchronous request.

sections.heading: 5. Make users wait less
6. Recommendation
sections.text: Define latency SLOs by task class and quality target. Never trade correctness or safety for speed without making that trade explicit.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Parallelism is useful when work is independent and resources permit it. It is harmful when it duplicates work, increases contention, or creates coordination debt.

sections.heading: 2. Parallelization test
3. Throughput vs latency
sections.text: High throughput and low single-task latency are different goals. Batch/offline work may maximize throughput while intentionally increasing individual completion time.

sections.heading: 4. Resource limits
sections.text: Model APIs, databases, browsers, sandboxes, package registries, and client systems all have independent quotas. Concurrency policy should protect downstream services rather than merely maximize model utilization.

sections.heading: 5. Backpressure
sections.text: Use queues, concurrency caps, admission control, and cancellation. Do not allow a spike of agent fan-out to create an uncontrolled cost or service cascade.

sections.heading: 6. Duplicate work
sections.text: Before spawning parallel agents, define ownership and shared findings. Detect overlapping exploration when practical.

sections.heading: 7. Recommendation
sections.text: Use bounded parallelism and measure end-to-end wall time, total cost, duplicate effort, and failure rate together.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Reuse previously performed work when semantics allow it. Choose the reuse mechanism according to freshness, latency, and isolation requirements.

sections.heading: 2. Prompt caching
sections.text: Prompt caching can materially reduce repeated-prefix cost and latency, especially for agent sessions with stable instructions, tools, and long histories. Preserve stable prefixes but do not retain irrelevant context merely to maximize cache hit rate.

sections.heading: 3. Application caching
4. Batch processing
5. Flex/low-priority processing
sections.text: Where supported, slower/interruptible processing may further reduce cost for lower-priority work. Treat availability and deadline constraints explicitly.

sections.heading: 6. Reuse boundaries
sections.text: Never reuse across incompatible security, scope, model-version, repository-version, or freshness scopes.

sections.heading: 7. Recommendation
sections.text: Use caching and batching as workload-level architecture decisions. Measure realized hit rate and net savings rather than assuming theoretical discounts will materialize.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Autonomous systems require explicit economic boundaries just as they require authority boundaries.

sections.heading: 2. Budget dimensions
sections.text:
Budgets may be expressed as:

```text
currency / task
currency / scope / month
tokens / task
model calls / task
tool calls / task
subagents / task
wall time / task
retry count
human-review minutes
```

sections.heading: Soft limit
sections.text: Trigger adaptation: smaller model, reduced fan-out, delayed enrichment, or explicit user notice where appropriate.

sections.heading: Hard limit
sections.text: Stop, checkpoint, or require authorization. Do not silently exceed a configured ceiling.

sections.heading: 4. Risk-adjusted budgets
sections.text: Higher-risk or higher-value work may justify more compute. A trivial formatting task and a production incident should not share identical budgets.

sections.heading: 5. Runaway prevention
6. Tenant/permission isolation
sections.text: Budgets and accounting should be separable by scope or business boundary where required. One tenant must not consume another's quota.

sections.heading: 7. Recommendation
sections.text: Treat economic limits as external policy enforced by the harness/platform, not as suggestions encoded only in prompts.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Optimization claims must be evaluated against representative tasks and repeated runs.

sections.heading: 2. Multi-objective comparison
3. Pareto frontier
sections.text:
A configuration is dominated if another configuration is no worse on all relevant objectives and better on at least one.

Prefer presenting the non-dominated frontier rather than declaring one universal winner.

sections.heading: 4. Experiment isolation
sections.text:
Change one architectural variable at a time where possible:

```text
model
reasoning effort
retrieval depth
reranking
context strategy
parallelism
cache policy
tool design
```

Otherwise causal interpretation becomes weak.

sections.heading: 5. Real workload weighting
sections.text: Aggregate scores should reflect expected workload distribution. Avoid optimizing heavily for rare benchmark tasks at the expense of routine engineering work.

sections.heading: 6. Optimization regression
sections.text: A cost reduction is unacceptable when it causes meaningful degradation in safety, correctness, or maintainability outside the experiment's headline metric.

sections.heading: 7. Recommendation
sections.text: Promote an optimization into handbook guidance only after it improves the relevant quality/cost/latency frontier for representative workloads.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Cost/performance assumptions decay quickly. Model prices, cache rates, rate limits, context behavior, default reasoning effort, batch discounts, and infrastructure characteristics all change.

sections.heading: 2. What must be versioned
sections.text:
Record where applicable:

```text
provider
model/version
pricing date
reasoning configuration
cache policy
processing tier
rate-limit tier
harness version
retrieval/index version
sandbox resources
tool versions
```

sections.heading: 3. Review cadence
4. Event-driven revalidation
5. Capacity planning
6. Remove obsolete optimizations
sections.text: An optimization introduced for an older model or pricing regime must have explicit revalidation/removal criteria. Cheap cached input, faster models, improved native tool use, or larger reliable contexts can invalidate prior architecture.

sections.heading: 7. Recommendation
sections.text: Treat cost/performance guidance as living operational knowledge backed by telemetry and recurring benchmarks.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Evaluation converts agent engineering from intuition into evidence. An eval is not merely a benchmark score; it is a repeatable mechanism for deciding whether a system satisfies a defined requirement under a defined environment.

sections.heading: 2. Core principle
sections.text:
**Evaluate the system that will actually be used.** For an agent, the evaluated unit is usually the model plus instructions, tools, retrieval, harness, environment, permissions, retries, and verification policy.

A model-only score is useful evidence, but it is not automatically evidence about the deployed agent.

sections.heading: 3. Outcome first, trace second
sections.text:
the platform should separate two questions:

1. **Outcome:** Did the task actually succeed in the environment?
2. **Process:** Did the agent reach that outcome safely, efficiently, and according to policy?

For coding agents, executable end-state checks are usually stronger than textual self-reports. Trace grading is then used to diagnose tool choice, handoffs, retries, policy violations, and wasted work.

sections.heading: 4. Evaluation dimensions
5. Eval-driven development
sections.text: New capabilities should increasingly be specified by examples and success criteria before they are considered mature. Early manual testing is acceptable, but recurring behavior should move toward repeatable evaluation as soon as it influences architecture or production commitments.

sections.heading: 6. Living knowledge
sections.text:
Eval failures are candidate knowledge. A recurring production failure should be eligible to become:

```text
production observation
      ↓
reproducible eval task
      ↓
fix / experiment
      ↓
regression protection
      ↓
handbook guidance
```

sections.heading: 7. Anti-patterns
1. Purpose
sections.text: A useful eval begins with an observable definition of success. The desired end state should be specified independently from whatever explanation the model gives about its own performance.

sections.heading: 2. Outcome hierarchy
sections.text:
Prefer the strongest available evidence:

```text
real environment state
    ↓
executable tests / invariants
    ↓
structured assertions
    ↓
reference comparison
    ↓
model judgment
    ↓
human subjective review
```

This is not a value judgment about humans; it reflects reproducibility and automation. Subjective product quality may legitimately require human review.

sections.heading: 3. Multi-dimensional success
4. Partial credit
sections.text: Use partial scores only where gradations are meaningful. Safety-critical requirements, destructive-operation constraints, and mandatory policy checks are often better represented as hard gates.

sections.heading: 5. Outcome loopholes
sections.text: Agents can discover unexpected paths that satisfy a brittle grader while violating intent. Graders should therefore encode the real requirement rather than proxies whenever practical, and suspiciously high scores should be inspected for reward hacking.

sections.heading: 6. Recommendation
1. Purpose
sections.text: An eval suite is only as representative as its tasks. Dataset design should reflect the real distribution of work while deliberately including important edge, failure, and adversarial cases.

sections.heading: 2. Dataset sources
3. Split the corpus
4. Diversity requirements
5. Difficulty distribution
sections.text: A useful suite contains easy, normal, hard, and pathological cases. If every task is currently solved near 100%, the suite provides little signal for capability improvement; if almost nothing succeeds, it provides weak regression signal.

sections.heading: 6. Production representativeness
sections.text: Track the difference between benchmark distribution and actual work. Public coding benchmarks are valuable comparators but must not substitute for the platform/scope-specific workloads.

sections.heading: 7. Task versioning
sections.text: Tasks are versioned artifacts. Changes to instructions, fixtures, tests, dependencies, or environments can invalidate historical comparisons and must be recorded.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Graders translate success criteria into repeatable measurements. the platform should use the simplest grader that faithfully measures the requirement.

sections.heading: 2. Grader hierarchy
3. LLM-as-judge
4. Multi-grader design
sections.text:
A task can combine hard gates and soft quality metrics. Example:

```text
unit tests                 hard gate
security policy            hard gate
unnecessary diff size      metric
architecture quality       calibrated judge
cost                       metric
latency                    metric
```

sections.heading: 5. Reward hacking
sections.text: A grader is part of the system and can be gamed. Inspect unexpectedly high-scoring outputs, keep hidden cases where justified, and avoid proxy metrics that are easier to satisfy than the actual requirement.

sections.heading: 6. Scoring policy
sections.text: Do not collapse all dimensions into one score unless the weighting reflects an actual decision. Preserve component metrics so a system cannot hide a critical regression behind gains elsewhere.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: End-state success is necessary but insufficient for autonomous systems. Trace evaluation examines the path: decisions, model calls, tool calls, handoffs, approvals, retries, and context transitions.

sections.heading: 2. What traces are for
3. Outcome vs trace
sections.text: A trace grader should not replace end-state verification. An agent may follow a beautiful process and still fail the task, or succeed while violating authority constraints.

sections.heading: 4. Trace schema
5. Trace mining
sections.text: Production traces should feed the living eval corpus. Recurring behavior clusters, rare failures, and high-cost paths are candidates for new regression tasks.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Agent results are stochastic. A single trial is evidence about one run, not a reliable estimate of a system's expected behavior.

sections.heading: 2. Repeated trials
3. Paired comparison
sections.text: When comparing two configurations, use the same task set and environment. Paired analysis is generally more informative than comparing unrelated aggregate runs.

sections.heading: 4. Infrastructure noise
sections.text:
Agentic coding results depend on CPU, memory, network, dependency availability, timeouts, sandbox behavior, and harness implementation. Environment differences can exceed the apparent performance difference between models.

Therefore, record and control infrastructure whenever the experiment claims comparative performance.

sections.heading: 5. Practical significance
sections.text: Statistical significance does not imply operational value. A 0.5% gain may not justify doubled cost; a small average gain may be extremely valuable if concentrated in high-risk tasks.

sections.heading: 6. Recommendation
sections.text:
For major architecture/model changes, require both:
- evidence that the difference is unlikely to be noise; and
- evidence that the difference matters to the decision being made.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Correctness is not the only operational objective. Agent systems consume model tokens, tool calls, compute, network time, and human attention.

sections.heading: 2. Metrics
3. Normalize by success
sections.text:
Cheap failures are not efficient. Prefer metrics such as:

```text
cost per successful task
latency at target success rate
human minutes per accepted result
```

rather than raw average token cost alone.

sections.heading: 4. Pareto analysis
sections.text: When systems trade quality against cost/latency, report a frontier rather than one universal winner. Different workload classes can rationally choose different operating points.

sections.heading: 5. Tail behavior
sections.text: Track p90/p95 latency and high-cost outliers. Agent loops can have acceptable averages while occasionally entering expensive pathological trajectories.

sections.heading: 6. Recommendation
sections.text: Every experiment that proposes an optimization should report quality and cost/latency together unless one is provably irrelevant.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text:
Capability tests and regression tests serve different purposes.

- **Capability evals** ask what the system can do and may intentionally begin with low pass rates.
- **Regression evals** protect behavior that is expected to remain stable.

sections.heading: 2. Promotion path
sections.text:
A useful lifecycle is:

```text
new behavior
   ↓
capability eval
   ↓
reliable enough for product use
   ↓
selected cases promoted to regression suite
```

sections.heading: 3. Release gates
4. Change-specific suites
sections.text: Model upgrade, prompt change, skill change, retrieval change, and tool schema change may need different targeted suites. Running everything on every commit may be wasteful; use layered CI where appropriate.

sections.heading: 5. Canary and production monitoring
sections.text: Offline evals cannot fully represent production. For consequential changes, combine pre-release evals with controlled rollout, trace monitoring, user feedback, and rollback criteria.

sections.heading: 6. Recommendation
sections.text: Every recurring production defect should be considered for conversion into a regression case if it can be reproduced safely and without retaining sensitive scoped data.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Human evaluation supplies domain intent and calibrates automated graders. It is especially important when quality is subjective, consequences are high, or the grader itself is being changed.

sections.heading: 2. Rubric design
3. Agreement
sections.text:
Measure reviewer agreement on a calibration subset. Disagreement can indicate ambiguous requirements rather than reviewer error.

Use adjudication for consequential cases and update the rubric when disagreement reveals unclear criteria.

sections.heading: 4. Calibrating model judges
5. Blind comparison
sections.text: Where possible, hide model/provider identity from human judges and randomize candidate order to reduce expectation bias.

sections.heading: 6. Recommendation
sections.text: Automated judges may replace large volumes of repetitive human scoring only after agreement is demonstrated for the exact rubric/workload. Human review remains the authority for redefining what the rubric should mean.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: A system that succeeds on benign tasks but fails under adversarial or malformed inputs is not production-ready for consequential use.

sections.heading: 2. Security eval classes
3. Environment containment
sections.text: Evaluate both model behavior and enforcement boundaries. The question is not only “does the agent refuse?” but also “can the environment prevent the action if the agent fails to refuse?”

sections.heading: 4. Negative capability
sections.text: Evals should verify that the system can correctly decline, escalate, request approval, or stop when required. Success is sometimes **not acting**.

sections.heading: 5. Adversarial maintenance
sections.text: Adversarial sets decay as attacks and model defenses evolve. Add real incident patterns, vendor advisories, and red-team findings to the living corpus.

sections.heading: 6. Recommendation
sections.text: Security-critical release gates should prefer objective state/permission checks over solely model-based safety judgments.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Evaluation infrastructure must make comparisons reproducible enough to support engineering decisions without pretending stochastic systems are perfectly deterministic.

sections.heading: 2. Required run metadata
3. Isolation
sections.text: Each trial should start from a known state. Coding evals should use reproducible repositories/containers and reset mutated state between trials.

sections.heading: 4. Provider-neutral core
sections.text:
the platform should own canonical task specifications, expected outcomes, run metadata, and result schema. Provider-specific eval products can be adapters rather than the source of truth.

This is especially important because vendor eval surfaces can change or be deprecated.

sections.heading: 5. Artifact retention
6. Minimal initial harness
sections.text:
Do not overbuild. Start with:

```text
task loader
runner
trace recorder
grader interface
result schema
comparison report
```

Add distributed execution, dashboards, and advanced scheduling only when workload requires them.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.text: Eval suites themselves become stale. Models improve, production distributions shift, tools change, tasks leak into training data, and formerly discriminating tests saturate.

sections.heading: 2. Living-eval lifecycle
3. Revalidation triggers
4. Benchmark hygiene
sections.text: Public benchmarks are useful external anchors but should not become the sole basis for internal decisions. Record benchmark version, harness, environment, and whether the tested system could have been explicitly optimized for the benchmark.

sections.heading: 5. Preventing test overfitting
sections.text: Maintain holdouts where useful, rotate tasks, derive fresh cases from production, and distinguish exploratory tuning sets from final comparison sets.

sections.heading: 6. Knowledge promotion
7. Vendor-tool freshness
sections.text: Vendor eval products are implementation choices, not handbook foundations. For example, OpenAI's legacy Evals platform is scheduled for shutdown on November 30, 2026; the platform guidance should therefore describe evaluation concepts and portable artifacts rather than couple organizational knowledge to one product surface.

sections.heading: Baseline Knowledge Inventory
sections.text:
The initial corpus covers context engineering, tool/MCP design, model routing, agent architecture, software-engineering agents, evaluation, security and authority, cost/performance, reusable skills, knowledge services, source intelligence, permission-aware retrieval, innovation, security assurance, and knowledge auditability.

This inventory is descriptive, not proof that every recommendation is mature.

sections.heading: Maturity rule
sections.text: Each topic must retain its own status, evidence, freshness, and experiment links. Presence in the handbook does not imply approval.

sections.heading: Initial implementation priorities
the platform Agent Engineering Glossary
sections.text: This glossary establishes working meanings for overloaded terms. Definitions are intentionally provider-neutral unless explicitly noted.

sections.heading: Agent
sections.text: A software system in which a model can select or sequence actions in pursuit of a goal using context, state, tools, and environmental feedback. An agent is more than a single model invocation.

sections.heading: Agent harness
sections.text: The runtime and control layer surrounding a model that manages instructions, context, state, tool invocation, permissions, retries, budgets, tracing, and termination.

sections.heading: Agentic workflow
sections.text: A workflow containing one or more agent-controlled decisions or action loops. Not every workflow that uses an LLM is agentic.

sections.heading: Autonomy
sections.text: The degree to which a system may select and execute actions without contemporaneous human approval. Autonomy is distinct from authority.

sections.heading: Authority
sections.text: The actions and resources a system is permitted to access or modify. A highly autonomous agent can still have narrowly scoped authority.

sections.heading: Context
sections.text: The information available to a model for a specific inference or reasoning step, including instructions, messages, retrieved information, tool results, state, summaries, and other supplied data.

sections.heading: Context engineering
sections.text: The discipline of selecting, structuring, retrieving, transforming, prioritizing, and managing the information available to a model over the lifecycle of a task.

sections.heading: Context window
sections.text: The maximum model-visible token capacity for an invocation or session as defined by the model/runtime. Usable context quality is not equivalent to raw context-window size.

sections.heading: Compaction
sections.text: A process that reduces accumulated context while attempting to preserve information required for future task progress.

sections.heading: Working memory
sections.text: Short-lived state required to continue the current task or session. Working memory may be stored outside the model context and selectively reintroduced.

sections.heading: Persistent memory
sections.text: Information retained beyond the immediate task or session for possible use later. Persistent memory requires explicit decisions about scope, trust, freshness, retrieval, and deletion.

sections.heading: Retrieval
sections.text: The process of selecting potentially relevant information from an external corpus or data source for use by an agent or model.

sections.heading: RAG
sections.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation. A broad pattern in which retrieved external information is supplied to a generative model. RAG is not synonymous with vector search.

sections.heading: Lexical retrieval
sections.text: Retrieval based on textual matching and term statistics, such as BM25. It is often strong for exact identifiers, symbols, names, and technical terms.

sections.heading: Semantic retrieval
sections.text: Retrieval based on learned semantic representations, commonly embeddings, intended to find conceptually related information even when exact words differ.

sections.heading: Hybrid retrieval
sections.text: A retrieval strategy that combines lexical and semantic approaches, usually followed by candidate merging and sometimes reranking.

sections.heading: Embedding
sections.text: A numerical representation of content in a vector space intended to preserve useful semantic or structural relationships for similarity search or related operations.

sections.heading: Reranker
sections.text: A model or algorithm that reorders a candidate set produced by an earlier retrieval stage using a more expensive or more precise relevance estimate.

sections.heading: Chunk
sections.text: A retrievable unit of content. Chunking strategy determines how documents, code, conversations, or other sources are divided for indexing and retrieval.

sections.heading: Progressive disclosure
sections.text: Providing information or capabilities only when the current task indicates they are needed rather than loading everything into context upfront.

sections.heading: Tool
sections.text: A callable capability exposed to an agent, usually with defined inputs, outputs, and authority. Examples include repository inspection, shell execution, database queries, or issue retrieval.

sections.heading: Tool call
sections.text: A single invocation of a tool by an agent or model.

sections.heading: MCP
sections.text: Model Context Protocol. A protocol for exposing tools, resources, prompts, and related capabilities to compatible AI clients. In the platform architecture, MCP is considered an interface rather than the canonical owner of organizational knowledge.

sections.heading: Skill
sections.text: A packaged, reusable capability that may include instructions, references, examples, templates, scripts, schemas, and evaluations. A skill should be scoped to a recognizable activity and support progressive disclosure where possible.

sections.heading: Instruction
sections.text: Authoritative guidance intended to influence agent behavior. Instructions should be distinguished from untrusted content that merely contains imperative language.

sections.heading: Prompt
sections.text: Text or structured content supplied to a model for an invocation. Prompts are one component of context, not the whole context-engineering discipline.

sections.heading: System instruction
sections.text: High-authority instruction supplied by the runtime or application to establish global behavior and constraints.

sections.heading: Repository instruction
sections.text: Stable guidance stored with a codebase or project to describe local conventions, commands, boundaries, and routing to deeper knowledge.

sections.heading: State
sections.text: Structured information representing relevant facts about the current workflow, environment, decisions, progress, or pending actions.

sections.heading: Trace
sections.text: A structured record of an agent run including model invocations, tool calls, transitions, errors, approvals, retries, state changes, timing, and related telemetry.

sections.heading: Eval
sections.text: A repeatable test or measurement used to assess agent or model behavior against defined criteria.

sections.heading: Grader
sections.text: A mechanism that scores or classifies an eval result. A grader may be deterministic, model-based, rule-based, or human.

sections.heading: Benchmark
sections.text: A standardized set of tasks or measurements intended to compare systems under controlled conditions. Benchmark results are meaningful only with sufficient detail about models, versions, environments, and methodology.

sections.heading: Experiment
sections.text: A controlled investigation designed to test a hypothesis or compare alternative approaches.

sections.heading: Model routing
sections.text: Selecting a model or mechanism based on characteristics such as task class, difficulty, cost, latency, risk, context requirements, or prior failures.

sections.heading: Escalation
sections.text: Moving from a lower-cost or lower-capability mechanism to a more capable one because evidence indicates that the current mechanism is insufficient.

sections.heading: Frontier model
sections.text: A model near the current state of the art in broad capability. The term is time-sensitive and should not be treated as a permanent model category tied to any vendor.

sections.heading: Small model
sections.text: A comparatively lower-cost, lower-latency model suited to bounded or high-volume tasks when its capability is sufficient. "Small" is relative and time-sensitive.

sections.heading: Specialist model
sections.text: A model optimized or selected for a narrower task class, such as embeddings, reranking, classification, speech, vision, or domain-specific processing.

sections.heading: Planner/executor
sections.text: An architecture that separates higher-level task planning from lower-level action execution. The roles may be separate agents, separate model calls, or explicit phases within one agent.

sections.heading: Generator/critic
sections.text: An architecture where one process produces an artifact and another critiques or evaluates it, often iteratively. The critic may be another model, the same model in a separate role, a deterministic validator, or a human.

sections.heading: Subagent
sections.text: An agent invoked by another agent or orchestrator to perform a scoped subtask, often with isolated context or authority.

sections.heading: Orchestration
sections.text: The coordination of models, agents, tools, state transitions, retries, handoffs, and workflow execution.

sections.heading: Human in the loop
sections.text: A workflow in which one or more steps require human input, review, approval, or decision before execution may continue.

sections.heading: Human on the loop
sections.text: A workflow in which a system can operate autonomously within limits while a human supervises, audits, or can intervene.

sections.heading: Prompt injection
sections.text: An attempt, intentional or accidental, for untrusted content to influence agent behavior as though it were authorized instruction.

sections.heading: Least privilege
sections.text: The principle of granting only the minimum permissions and authority necessary to perform the current task.

sections.heading: Sandbox
sections.text: An isolated execution environment intended to limit the impact of agent-executed code or actions.

sections.heading: Provenance
sections.text: Metadata describing where knowledge, guidance, evidence, or data came from, including source, version, scope, status, and lineage where relevant.

sections.heading: Overlay
sections.text: A scoped layer of guidance that augments or overrides more general knowledge, such as project-, repository-, or task-specific standards.

sections.heading: Effective guidance
sections.text: The resolved set of instructions, standards, recommendations, and constraints applicable to a specific task after relevant overlays and precedence rules are considered.

sections.heading: Deterministic verification
sections.text: Validation performed by a mechanism expected to produce the same result for the same input, such as compilation, schema validation, a unit test, or a static-analysis rule.

sections.heading: Model-based verification
sections.text: Validation performed by an LLM or other probabilistic model. Useful where deterministic checks cannot fully capture the requirement, but generally weaker than deterministic evidence for objectively testable properties.

sections.heading: Agentic repair loop
sections.text: A bounded cycle in which an agent executes work, observes environmental feedback or verification failures, diagnoses the issue, modifies the work, and verifies again.

sections.heading: Budget
sections.text: A limit on resources an agent may consume, such as model calls, tokens, time, tool calls, retries, money, or privileged actions.

sections.heading: Mission
sections.text:
Maintain a secure, evidence-backed, living engineering knowledge system for designing, evaluating, and operating agentic software-engineering systems.

The platform is knowledge-first. It improves engineering decisions and agent behavior through structured guidance, source intelligence, experiments, reusable skills, permission-aware retrieval, and security assurance.

sections.heading: AEP-P-001 — Earn Every Model Call
sections.text: A model call should provide value that simpler deterministic code, retrieval, caching, or reuse cannot provide as reliably.

sections.heading: AEP-P-002 — Earn Every Agent
sections.text: Use additional agents only when decomposition, isolation, parallelism, or specialization creates measurable benefit.

sections.heading: AEP-P-003 — Context Is a Finite Engineering Resource
sections.text: Construct the smallest sufficient context and protect it from irrelevant, stale, or unauthorized material.

sections.heading: AEP-P-004 — Retrieve Evidence; Let the Agent Reason
sections.text: Prefer retrieving authoritative evidence and letting the model reason over it rather than storing generated answers as truth.

sections.heading: AEP-P-005 — Prefer Tools Over Descriptions of Tools
sections.text: When a stable capability exists, expose it as a structured tool instead of repeatedly teaching the model to simulate it.

sections.heading: AEP-P-006 — Deterministic Systems Establish Ground Truth
sections.text: Use compilers, tests, schemas, policy checks, security controls, and postconditions for objective verification.

sections.heading: AEP-P-007 — Verification Is Part of Execution
sections.text: A task is not complete merely because an agent reports completion; verification belongs in the workflow.

sections.heading: AEP-P-008 — Measure Before Optimizing
sections.text: Instrument quality, cost, latency, reliability, and human intervention before optimizing architecture.

sections.heading: AEP-P-009 — Optimize Quality, Cost, and Latency Together
sections.text: Treat these dimensions as a frontier rather than optimizing one in isolation.

sections.heading: AEP-P-010 — Escalate Capability Instead of Defaulting to It
sections.text: Begin with the least expensive adequate configuration and escalate when external evidence indicates the need.

sections.heading: AEP-P-011 — Agents Operate Under Explicit Authority
sections.text: Agent capability and authority are separate. Permission boundaries must be explicit.

sections.heading: AEP-P-012 — Untrusted Content Is Data, Not Instruction
sections.text: Retrieved documents, repository content, tool output, and other external text do not gain instruction authority by entering context.

sections.heading: AEP-P-013 — Preserve Provenance
sections.text: Important claims, guidance, artifacts, and decisions remain traceable to their sources and versions.

sections.heading: AEP-P-014 — Separate Knowledge From Interfaces
sections.text: Canonical knowledge and domain logic must not be owned by MCP, CLI, IDE, or provider-specific adapters.

sections.heading: AEP-P-015 — Prefer Portable Knowledge Over Vendor Lock-In
sections.text: Keep workflows, contracts, evals, and knowledge portable while allowing adapters to exploit useful provider-specific capabilities.

sections.heading: AEP-P-016 — Observe the Environment Before Prescribing Infrastructure
sections.text: Use repository and enterprise capabilities already present before introducing new orchestration, indexing, build, or runtime layers.

sections.heading: AEP-P-017 — Living Knowledge Must Be Revalidated
sections.text: Guidance, model assumptions, tools, sources, and workarounds require scheduled and event-driven review.

sections.heading: AEP-P-018 — Deterministic Control Before Agentic Control
sections.text: Use deterministic orchestration and policy where behavior is known; introduce agentic control only where reasoning materially helps.

sections.heading: AEP-P-019 — Prefer Environmental Fit Over Organizational Familiarity
sections.text: Familiar technologies may improve implementation speed but must not override workload, ecosystem, security, operational, maintainability, or cost constraints.

sections.heading: AEP-P-020 — Evals Are Executable Requirements
sections.text: Recurring important behavior should increasingly be represented by repeatable evaluation rather than prose alone.

sections.heading: AEP-P-021 — Authority Must Be Enforced Outside the Model
sections.text: Identity, authorization, sandbox boundaries, approvals, and destructive-action controls must be enforced by systems the model cannot redefine.

sections.heading: AEP-P-022 — Optimize Cost Per Useful Outcome
sections.text: Optimize accepted successful outcomes under quality and security constraints rather than raw tokens or request price.

sections.heading: AEP-P-023 — Skills Operationalize Knowledge; They Do Not Own It
sections.text: Skills package reusable procedures and assets while canonical standards remain in authoritative sources.

sections.heading: AEP-P-024 — Canonical Knowledge and Derived Intelligence Must Remain Distinct
sections.text: Indexes, embeddings, summaries, rankings, and context packages are derived and rebuildable from canonical reviewed sources.

sections.heading: AEP-P-025 — Permission Boundaries Apply Before Retrieval
sections.text: Authorization constrains the eligible corpus before retrieval, ranking, synthesis, caching, or context construction.

sections.heading: AEP-P-026 — Vendor Concepts Belong at the Edge
sections.text: The core models enterprise capabilities; vendor products are optional adapters.

sections.heading: AEP-P-027 — Observable Behavior, Not Anthropomorphic Interpretation
sections.text: Security and behavioral assurance evaluate concrete policy and invariant violations rather than inferred model intent.

sections.heading: AEP-P-028 — Evidence Before Promotion
sections.text: Information moves through explicit maturity and review states before it becomes normative guidance.

sections.heading: Knowledge status
sections.text:
Canonical knowledge uses explicit statuses:

```text
approved
recommended
provisional
experimental
informational
deprecated
rejected
```

Status, authority, freshness, scope, trust, and relevance remain separate properties.

sections.heading: Initial implementation boundary
sections.text:
The initial implementation is read-oriented and knowledge-first:

```text
canonical knowledge
source intelligence
permission-aware retrieval
evaluation
skills
auditability
CLI
read-only MCP
```

An enterprise SDLC control plane is intentionally deferred until the platform has produced operational evidence.

sections.heading: Sequence
Governing rule
sections.text: Do not jump ahead because a later subsystem is more interesting. Each stage should create evidence that informs the next.

sections.heading: Open Questions
sections.text: This document tracks unresolved questions that can materially change platform guidance.

sections.heading: Knowledge and retrieval
sections.text:
- What metadata fields materially improve downstream task success?
- When do embeddings and reranking improve results beyond lexical/structural retrieval?
- What context-package size maximizes useful outcome per cost?
- Which freshness labels measurably change agent behavior?

sections.heading: Permission boundaries
sections.text:
- What scope model is expressive enough for people and service identities without making retrieval brittle?
- How should caches and indexes isolate restricted scopes?
- Which authorization decisions require durable audit records?

sections.heading: Source intelligence
sections.text:
- How should authority, recency, corroboration, and reproducibility combine without becoming an opaque trust score?
- Which source-discovery techniques achieve acceptable precision?

sections.heading: Skills
sections.text:
- When does a skill outperform repository guidance?
- How should skill catalogs scale without activation noise?

sections.heading: Security assurance
sections.text:
- Which adversarial suites best predict real agent-system failures?
- How should fintech-grade automated penetration testing remain isolated and governable?

sections.heading: Future architecture
sections.text:
- Which production policy engine best fits the eventual enterprise authorization model?
- What lessons from platform operation should drive a future SDLC control-plane redesign?

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text: The platform should create new engineering knowledge, not merely retrieve established practice. Novel ideas enter through a governed hypothesis-and-experiment pipeline.

sections.heading: Guidance
sections.text:
- Novelty is not evidence.
- Prefer falsifiable hypotheses.
- Keep experimental work isolated from normative guidance.
- Record failed experiments as useful negative knowledge.
- Promotion requires measured benefit.
